It is crib work joined by bridges. It extends out about 700 or 800 feet.
Is this wharf to be longer than 700 feet?
I have not the details of the new wharf. * The site will have to be changed as there is no water at the old site of the old wharf.
I am sorry I cannot give the length of the wharf.
Surely the minister is not asking for a vote without knowing how far the wharf will extend?
I can give specifications of the plan it is now proposed to adopt. First, we are to improve the road down to the foot of the hill at the shore line.
How far inland does that shore extend?
Just down the bank to the wharf.
Is that a private municipal road?

It will be a public road. Then we will have a crib roadway of timber and stone to the foot of the hill, 85,000 cubic feet; new intermediate block 100 by 22 by 17 equals 87,400 cubic feet; head block average 2124 by 524 by 19 equals 211,964 cubic feet; new trestle roadway 500 feet which will be capable of being removed in the fall. That gives a very good idea in a general way of the extent of the wharf.
In whom is the fee of the roadway leading down to the wharf?
In the government.
Are the approaches to the wharf and the title of the land on which the wharf will be built, in the government?
All in the government.
Will this interfere with the private wharf at which the vessels call at present?
No, that other wharf is twenty-five miles away. When this wharf is built the steamers which call at the other wharf will call at it.

I wish to know from the minister whether he will entertain with respect to other localities of the same size and importance as this, an application for a wharf that would involve a like expenditure? I have two localities in my riding which have been petitioning for satisfactory wharfs and which cannot get them because the minister seems to think that the expense involved would be too large in proportion to the importance of the district to be served. I have listened very attentively to all the descriptions given of the importance of this district, and as I have said with respect to the other items, if it is a proper item I am certainly not opposed to it. I have heard the minister state that on account of the peculiar situation of this place it unfortunately takes a large expenditure to provide the accommodation, which of course it should have. I quite admit that this locality should have an effective shipping wharf, but I would like the minister to say whether I understood his principle correctly to be, that a wharf should be provided at any cost if a locality needed it. If that is the principle I want to apply^ it in another direction. Is that the principle upon which the minister asks for this appropriation, and if so

is he willing to extend the principle to an application which I shall file when the proper time comes with respect to wharfs which he has withheld from us, because he thinks they will cost more than the trade of the place justified?

I have not said there was any such principle. The hon. gentleman seems to think that I said that where a wharf was to the public advantage it -would be built no matter what it would cost. I said nothing of the kind, and I never intended to lay down any such principle. What I said was that in this particular case, in view of the large number of people to be accommodated, in view of the report of the engineer, in view of the fact that the only reasonable means the people have of getting to market is by water, I thought we were justified in going to this expense. As to any application which my hon. friend has to submit I can give no promise and assurance whatever beyond this:	that whenever any application is
made I shall feel it my duty to consider the matter very carefully, and I must deal with each individual application upon its merits.

Am I to understand that if any damage results to a private or municipal interest by reason of the construction of a public work the department will make good that damage? I may say that I believe that is a proper principle. When the government was constructing the Trent canal there was a road running parallel to the canal between the counties of Victoria and Ontario; and those engaged in the construction threw the excavated sand on to the public road of the municipality, rendering it almost impassable. I understand that petitions have come to the department asking.for a grant in reference to the gravel road injured in this way on the Balsam division of the Trent canal. I hope the minister will take these petitions into his favourable consideration. The principle involved in this is the same as that which justifies the government in protecting Laprairie and other villages on the St. Lawrence which were injured by water backing up in consequence of certain work done by the harbour commissioners of Montreal. I would ask the minister-to make a grant to the municipalities to regravel that road.
I would have thought that my hon. friend had heard the Trent Valley canal discussed often enough in the House to know that it is in the Department of Railways and Canals, and not in my department.

I would like to ask the minister if his department has ever prepared a statement showing the length of life of these wharfs, and the expenditure for re-1354
newals per thousand dollars of cost of construction. This would be interesting information to have, because this is a growing expenditure, and it would give us some idea of where we stand with reference to the cost of wharfs throughout the country.

That has not been figured out.

House again in Committee of Supply.
St. Joseph de Sorel-wharf on west side of River Richelieu-revote of $3,000 lapsed, $9,000.
['We will proceed on Monday with the naval debate.']

This is to make provision towards the construction of a pile wharf on the west side of the River Riche-) lieu. There has been a petition for it sent; to the department. We expect this vote will finish the work. We had a vote fori the year ending March 31, 1909, which we did not use. This is a new work.
Sorel-deepwater wharf, $42,000.

We had a vote last year of $86,000, but we only expended $44,000 of it. We are simply asking now a revote of the appropriation of last year that was unexpended. This will complete the work.
Sorel-breakwater of pile work and stone filling opposite Elizabeth street-revote of $2,500 lapsed, $5,000.

This is to provide for the construction of a breakwater of pile and stone work. Nothing has yet been expended on this work. This is the total estimated cost. We took a partial vote for it and allowed it to lapse.
Tadousac harbour, north shore of St. Lawrence-wharf on southeast side of Tadousac island-revote of $4,600 lapsed, $15,000.

This is a new undertaking. The old wharf at Tadousac has got into a pretty bad condition, _ and has become dangerous. A new wharf is urgently required, and is expected to cost about

$[DOT]30,000. It will be crib-work filled with stone, and there will be a slip in it, and necessarily a shed upon it.
Three Rivers-deep water coal wharf at west end of harbour, opposite windmill-revote of $7,500 lapsed, $50,000.

This is to build a wharf which is very much needed at Three Rivers. We took a vote for the year 1908-9 of $7,500, but we did not proceed to let the contract, because the amount was too small to warrant us in entering into the contract without coming back to parliament. The pier which has been built there is required for ordinary merchandise, but there is no accommodation for the very large coal business. The harbour commissioners have urged this upon us, and the member for the county has also strongly urged it. I think also there are petitions for it; at all events, we had an interview by repre-* sentatives of Three Rivers, including the harbour commissioners. This will be a new work. We called for tenders for the work under the appropriation of 1908-9, but owing to the vote being so small, I declined to accept the tenders and returned the cheques. I cannot give the exact amount, but my impression is that the lowest ten-, der was in the vicinity of $140,000. The matter is entirely open, the deposit cheques having been returned. There is at Three Rivers a pier which was built in 1903-4, but that is for general merchandise, and it is fully occupied, so the engineer reports. This is for the purpose of enabling coal to be handled at the harbour. Three Rivers is a place of a good deal of importance. It is the outlet for Shawinigan Falls, some 20 miles away. Unfortunately, there was a severe fire at Three Rivers a year or more ago, which did the place a great deal of injury, but I am told it is building up rapidly again.
Is this for the purpose of bringing in coal?
Coal, and also to afford protection to boats frequenting the harbour.
Is it under a harbour master? .
There is a board of harbour commissioners at Three Rivers.

Would the minister inform us just what purpose this wharf is going to serve? Is it the practice of the government now to build wharfs for every municipality that desires that accommodation, or for any private individual who may say that he needs a wharf for his own purposes? Is the government going to lay down piers and build wharfs throughout the entire country wherever there is navigable water? Is the government assuming Mr. PUGSLEY.
not only the control of all the harbours, but also embarking in the enterprise of building piers wherever a harbour is to be used? If so it would seem to me that the government is laying up trouble for itself in the future both in regard to putting docks where there are no docks now, and as to perpetually keeping in repair docks and wharfs that they are now building. It seems , to be a new departure in the policy of the government. I would like to know from the minister if this dock is going to serve any general public purpose, or whether it is serving a local purpose, and what other docks there are? Are there public or private docks, if so are they under any commission, or is this government simply going to build wharfs and docks at that point?

It is a pretty difficult thing to answer my hon. friend categorically. We cannot lay down any definite rule as to what wharfs shall or shall not be built. For instance, at Fort William, the government is building a quay or wharf a good many hundreds of feet in length. We are doing that to facilitate the handling of merchandise, grain and coal.
That is a national lake port.

My hon. friend say3 it is a national port. I suppose he would say that the harbour of Toronto is a national port. So it is. You cannot say with certainty what is a national port and what is not. In the city of St. John I can well remember that the old government would not do any dredging in the harbour near any wharf because it would be said that they were benefiting the property of the city. They refused absolutely, stating that it was not part of their duty to do it.
So did this government.
Up to a certain date, but we have broadened out since then.
Lately, yes.
We have awakened to a clearer realization of the needs of this great country.
That is right.

And I do not think anybody will condemn us for doing it. The government are building a wharf at St. John to facilitate the handling of the business of Canada. I think my hon. friend will say that St. John is entitled to take its place as one of the national ports of Canada.
There is no doubt about that.

We believe it is, but at the same time there are numerous places throughout Ontario where we have built

and are building wharfs. If my hon. friend will go up to Lake Nipissing, to the Montreal river, to Sault Ste. Marie, and scores of other places in Ontario, he will find that we are building wharfs, not to accommodate any particular railway company or any particular coal or lumber company, but to facilitate the particular business which can be properly handled at that port. At Three Rivers what have we? We have a town of large importance. It is the port of Shaw-inigan, Grand Mere, and other thriving communities situated back from the St. Lawrence. At Three Rivers the coal business has reached enormous proportions. It amounts to 100,000 tons a year, and there is no place at that port where that coal business can be handled. We have a pier built by the government. We had hoped that would be sufficient for the different kinds of merchandise, including coal, but the Harbour Commissioners, the people and the engineers say, no, it is crowded with business, and we have felt that it would be proper to build this pier in order to give accommodation to the rapidly increasing business. I do not know just whom it will help most, but I should think that the community will be the most specially benefited because it will make Tiiree Rivers a very important distributing point for the coal which will be brought there from Nova Scotia and other parts. We do know that a large business is done there in Nova Scotia coal. A 100,000 tons a year, at least, will be distributed from Three Rivers if we give this required accommodation. As to the other question that my hon. friend asked, I may say that the pier which has been already built is placed under the control of the Harbour Commissioners, and this pier, when built, will also be placed under the Harbour Commissioners. I believe the work is a very important one, and if we recognize that it is our duty to assist in facilitating business we can justify to i the fullest extent the building of this wharf.
I understood the minister to say that the amount voted last year was so small that although tenders were invited none was accepted.
No.
Is it intended to advertise for tenders again or to act on any of the tenders received under the first call?

We have not decided the matter. There would be some reason why we should accept the lowest tender now provided the engineer is of opinion that, considering what difference there may be in the cost of material and wages to-day as compared with the time when the tenders were invited, the lowest tender
is fair and reasonable. We might accept that even at this late date because you will see there is some unfairness in rejecting tenders and then inviting them over again, providing the tenders are reasonable in each case. Therefore, all other things being equal, I would rather be disposed to favour the lowest tender now that we have decided to go on with the work.
If that is done is it intended to add to the amount of the tender the additional cost of labour and material compared with what it was when the tender was submitted?
No, if we accept the tender at all we will accept it as it is put in.
How many tenders did you receive for this work?
Six or seven.
I suppose it is too early to give the committee what the tenders are?
There would be no objection if I had them here, but my impression is that the lowest tender is somewhere in the vicinity of $140,000.
What was tne engineer's estimate of the work?
Between $7,000 and $10,000 higher than the lowest tender.
Is it fair to give that information?
He has not given us what the tenders are.

No, but the deposits have been returned and the lowest tender need not take it. It does not seem to me to be right that such information should go broadcast, if the department have any idea of dealing with the tenders that have been received by them for the simple reason that this knowledge is given to everybody and to the lowest tenderer that the department deem his figures too low.
Have the deposits been returned?
Yes.
Because if the deposits have been returned there is no obligation resting upon any of the tenderers to enter into a contract. It is entirely the option of the tenderer to take it or not.
That was stated some time ago.
Would the minister please state what work will be covered by the vote for Toronto harbour?

The principal work at Toronto is the building of the entrance to the western harbour which is a very important work. A contract was let for I think $490,000 odd and this vote is to pay the contractor. There is some additional work which we are doing on the pier near the eastern entrance and this vote will also provide for that. I believe the new western entrance is going to be of very great value to the harbour, and while it was costly, it will probably be worth more than its cost to the traffic coming to Toronto.

I agree with the minister as to the importance of the work and the necessity for it, and the wisdom of putting this appropriation in the estimates. The work at the western entrance is now being carried out on the basis of an 18 foot channel, and I believe it is the expectation that the inland waterways of the great lakes are to be standardized to a depth of 22 feet, as far as possible. The main harbours on the great lakes are I understand being deepened to 22 feet, and I would now suggest to the minister that the channel at Toronto be dredged to 22 feet instead of 18 feet as at present contemplated. I am informed that if the present contract is comnleted on the basis of an 18 foot channel it will in all probability have to be deepened in the near future, and that the increased cost of adding this depth after the present work is completed would be far greater than if the channel were deepened to 22 feet now. Would the minister state what is the intention of the department in this regard, and whether the opinion of the resident engineer has been obtained, which I think is a matter of considerable importance, he being on the ground and knowing all the circumstances?

It strikes me that it would be of no advantage to dredge to a greater depth than we are now dredging until the Welland canal be deepened, and even if that work were undertaken at an early date it would be some time before it could be completed. It seems to me there would be no greater difficulty in dredging the channel to the western entrance to a depth of 22 feet later on, than if we did it at present. I think the revetment walls at each side of the channel are sunk to a depth of 22 feet, but of that I am not absolutely sure, and at any future time the channel can be excavated to a greater depth between these walls just as well as it can be at the present time. I thank my hon. friend for the suggestion and I will have it looked into. I quite realize that in the future we must look to greater depth in our harbours. I am providing to-day for a 25 foot channel in Fort William and Port Arthur, and I am looking forward to having a depth of 25 feet in the harbours on Mr. MACDONELL.
the eastern shores of the Georgian bay, particularly at Tiffin and Victoria which are national harbours and which are so close-'.y allied with Fort William and Port Arthur. If we are going to hold our trade we must make our harbours deep enough to give accommodation to the largest lake vessels.
You would have to deepen the canal as well. ,
Yes.

The eastern entrance of the harbour requires immediate attention from the government. The eastern piers are rapidly decaying, and unless they are at once put in proper condition it will cost a very large sum to replace them later on. Will any part of this vote be devoted to that purpose?

We have done considerable work at the eastern entrance in the past season and the work has been very satisfactory. We intend to continue it during the coming season and we shall take what is required for the eastern channel out of this vote.

Toronto island has been practically washed away on one or two occasions and the breakwater is in urgent need of repair. Very excellent work has been performed there which has had the effect of protecting the island from the full sweep of the sea, and if that work is continued the island can be preserved. If steps are not taken now, not only will the island be in danger, but the work already done will be rendered entirely useless.

We have received a certificate and report from the city engineer of Toronto testifying to the very satisfactory way in which the work of finishing the breakwater has been done. As now completed it is proving very effective, and we believe, from the reports of our own engineer as well as those of the city engineer of Toronto, that it will give great satisfaction.

Is there any definite system of inspection or checking of the quantities of dredging done? I heard one of the engineers of the department admit on oath that in one case there were larger returns made by the inspector than the capacity of the scow, so that there must have been fraud or looseness or incompetence on the part of the inspector. Where millions of dollars are expended in these dredging contracts there should be competent and experienced inspectors, perhaps more than one on each boat continuously, to check the work properly.

I may say that we have a very thorough, and as we believe, a very

perfect system of inspection. We have recently made the rule more stringent than it was previously. We require the inspector to be constantly on the work, to personally inspect every scow load, to make his report and with it a solemn declaration that he has a personal knowledge of the quantity in every scow load. Having said that, let me appeal to my hon. friend not to believe one side of a story until he hears the other side, and not to be too ready to take insinuations which are made, but to look into the facts for himself. The hon. gentleman refers to some questions which were put by a certain member of this place. The gentleman who put these ques-House to the chief engineer in another tions assumed that the capacity of the scow was so many cubic yards.
The engineer said that.

No. I read the evidence, and he put the words into the engineer's mouth. As a matter of fact, upon that very work there were two additional scows which were hired by the contractors from the department, and which had a capacity of nearly 20 cubic yards greater than the quantity stated by the gentleman who examined the chief engineer. That fact explains the whole matter.
When was the new system of inspection inaugurated?
In 1908, about a year after I became minister.

I think the minister did not commence a moment too soon, because I have a very distinct recollection of a good many irregularities in connection with the dredging system. For instance, in one case an inspector was inspecting two dredges which were operating a quarter of a mile apart.
He was dismissed.

And he was at the time an employee of one of the dredging companies. it was admitted, I think, that it was utterly impossible for him to do his duty, but all the same payments were made on the returns he sent in.
Mt. PUGSLEY When I became minister in August, 1907, I took occasion to look into the matter carefully and to consider with my deputy what we could do to surround the dredging operations with the greatest possible safeguards; and in the following season we did adopt what we think are proper safeguards. We send out instructions in writing to the inspectors that if they do not give personal attention to the work they will be at once dismissed without notice, and we require them with each return to make a solemn declaration that they have been personally on the
work and have a personal knowledge of all the scow loads which were removed. In the case to which my hon. friend refers, the moment it came to the knowledge of the department that the inspector was attending to those two dredges we dismissed him.	[DOT]
What is the wage of the inspectors?
The wages vary, but the usual wage is $3 a day.
The inspectors are continuously on the dredge?
Yes.
What did the minister mean by saying that the member who questioned the chief engineer put the answer into his mouth? Did he suggest to the witness a certain capacity of the scow?

No; what I said was this: The member took the capacity of a certain scow and assumed that that was the capacity of all the scows, and asked the engineer how he accounted for it that 200 cubic yards were returned when the capacity of the scow was only 190 yards. The engineer said he could not account for it. As a matter of fact, at that time there where two other scows with a capacity of 210 cubic yards each.

I would like to draw the minister's attention to an application which I have made on two or three occasions to have a small wharf constructed at a place called Beaumarais, on the Muskoka lakes.
I do not find any item for it in the estimates. I hope the minister will take a note of it and make provision for it. Beaumarais is a very important point. The wharf is getting into a very dilapidated condition, and is very dangerous to the travelling public. If I told the minister the amount of tonnage that calls at that wharf he would be very much surprised.
May I ask the hon. gentleman if that is a private or a public wharf?

It was built originally by a private individual; but he has offered to hand it over to the .government free of charge if they will take it. They can get it by building a new wharf.
Manitoba-harbours, rivers and bridges- general repairs and improvements-$8,000.
This is the usual general vote taken every year to cover repairs to wharfs for which there is no special vote. It was $6,000 last year; we are asking for $8,000 this year.

I have watched the estimates come down from year to year since 1904, and I have failed to find any appro

priation for the completion of a wharf on Lake Manitoba, near St. Laurent. The government undertook to construct a wharf there in 1904, but they got it into their heads all at once that it was necessary to commence this piece of work without calling for tenders. They have expended almost $16,000; and so far as any value is concerned up to the present, that money might as well have been thrown into the fire. The work stands there a monument of the wonderful ability of this government to spend public money just before the elections. The people were promised that this would be carried to completion, but the day after the elections, the work ceased, the dredge was taken away and has not been sent back since; but I might tell the hon. minister that there was an election in 1908, which no doubt he remembers when the same parties, or some of them, went to these good people and said they regretted very much that this work had not been completed, but that it would certainly be gone on with provided the people voted for the government candidate. Well, the people did support the government candidate. In a particular poll where I got 28 of a majority in the election of 1904, my opponent got a majority of 65. Surely the people have done their duty. They took the government at their word on two occasions, and yet that piece of work stands there unfinished-not a dollar in the estimates or supplementaries to complete it, and it has so far cost the people uselessly $15,978. I would like to know if the minister still intends to leave that piece of work unfinished? I put a number of questions on the order paper this session regarding it which, in the absence of the Minister of Public Works, the Minister of Railways and Canals answered. They will be found on page 1240 of ' Hansard.' The Minister of Railways told the House that this was a piece of work in first-class condition, that it offered facilities to meet the public requirements in that locality and so on. But the fact is, we cannot get to that wharf. His answers, however, would lead the House to believe that you could get there with almost an ocean going vessel. Why, we cannot get there with anything larger than a canoe.

The work to which my hon. friend refers was evidently laid out upon a pretty large scale. It was begun in 1902 or 1903, and at that time it was expected that there would be considerable railway development in that locality, and also that a .large freezer would be established there, and it was proposed to build two piers on Lake Manitoba and dredge the channel between that and a lake nearby, and then have a wharf on the other side of the lake, which would be reached by a railway and where a freezer would be lo-Mr. STAPLES
cated. There were strongly signed petitions for this work, including one from the Board of Trade of Winnipeg The expenditure incurred has been made upon the piers in Lake Manitoba and also in dredging out the channel between the two lakes. By the plan it was intended to dredge across the lagoon and then build a wharf at the opposite side. Just at present, I am not impressed with the immediate necessity of doing that work, particularly in view of the fact that the large freezer contemplated has not been erected and that the expected railway development has not taken place. During the past year we have expended on those piers $513.13, and they are serving quite a useful purpose.

I do not know where the hon. minister has got his information as to the usefulness of that work. I have letters from various constituents living up there, and I have been there myself and have seen the work, and it is of no practical value. The minister says he is not particularly concerned about it and has no intention of continuing it. It would have been better if this government had taken their present view before spending $16,000 of the people's money for no practical use. But the work, if completed, would be of great practical value to the people of that district. So far as the freezer is concerned, would any sane person undertake to build a freezer, which might cost thousands of dollars, before he could get goods to utilize the freezer for any purpose? And so far as railway development is concerned, the Canadian Northern railway say they are quite ready to build a spur into this wharf as soon as it is built. The minister now says he does not propose appropriating any money to complete this work. What right then had these very keen politicians, before the election of 1908, to advise the people that if they would support the government candidate, this work would be completed?

My hon. friend makes statements as to certain alleged facts, of which I was not aware. He says that tHe railway company has agreed to do its part of this development work by building a spur to the water. So far as my information goes, we have no record of any such offer.

I do not know that it would be necessary that the department should have any record of what the company intend doing. The people of the district have the promise of that company that when this work is completed, a spur will be built.
During the last year or two we have been obliged to go somewhat slowly in public works.
You should also go slowly in promises.

My information is that the work done is very useful in connection with the shipping on Lake Manitoba. I have felt that it is not unreasonable that before going to the large expenditure necessary to dredge the lagoon and build a wharf on the other side we shouldjiave an assurance from the railway company that they would do their part towards the development of the locality. If the railway company would submit a memorandum of their willingness to, make the extension as soon as we built the wharf, the matter would have my most careful consideration.
On whose advice is the minister acting as to the usefulness of this work?
The advice I have is the information I received from the resident engineer, Mr. Dufresne, as to existing conditions.
Have you any letters containing that information? The people up there would foe glad to know just what it is.
If my hon. friend would convey to the people the answer at page 1240 of Hansard', he will see the statement made to the House and the representation of the resident engineer.

I have several litters from people in that district saying that the answer referred to is anything but accurate, and that if this wharf was completed there is no doubt the railway company would build the spur. I protest at the government expending $16,000 on a work that is of no practical use. It was spent when an election was pending to secure a' few votes, the people supported the government candidate and it is up to the Minister of Public Works to carry out the promise that was then made by somebody.

Nobody had my authority to make any statement in regard to this work. I was not aware that any such statements were being made and certainly never authorized any such statement. It would not be unreasonable that my hon. friend should ask the people to communicate with the railway company and ask whether they will engage to build this spur.

I desire to see this work completed, and I would think the government, to avoid the criticism they subject themselves to foy spending that _ money on a useless work, would be desirous of making it of some practical use.

It is curious that I have had no communication from any
people in the locality on the subject. It was represented that the Manitoba Fish Company and a Gypsum Company would make large shipments from here, but that has not been the case.
How could they when the work was not completed?

The piers could be used for a landing and if tne people wished the improvements it would be easy for them to have the Canadian Northern write me that they were prepared to build the spur and for these other companies to write that they would do their share.

I would expect the minister not to wait to ask the Canadian Northern railway or any other company what they propose to do but would send some one up to ascertain whether or not the work was of any value and then come here and tell us straight.
My engineer has been up theTe and has reported.
If the work was not worth completing it was not. worth starting, and the government should have had the necessary information before beginning it.
Is there any connection between the building of the freezers and the fishing companies who received the very cheap licenses?
Why did he spend $16,000 without an assurance from the company that they would build their share?

It was all done before I became minister, therefore, I cannot tell what assurances there were. But I would suppose that at the inception of this work there were assurances. Probably the fishermen said:	We are going right to
work and build the freezers. I suppose the Canadian Northern railway said: We are going to work and build the spur; and the Gypsum Company said:	We
will ship all our gypsum in that way. Then my predecessor, did the government part of the work, that is the only part that has been done. This Freezing Company has not materialized, this Gypsum Company has not attempted to ship any of their products, and the Canadian Northern railway has not begun to build its spur. Although I have been minister for nearly three years, I have not received a single word from those people, I have not received a single assurance that if we did go on and finish up this additional work, any of these things will materialize.
Would not these assurances still be in the department?
I do not know if they 1 are in the department or not.

I happen to know something about this district, although it is not in my constituency. I think if the minister understood the conditions there he would not hesitate for a moment in building that dock in such a way that it could be used. The dock is built in a position to-day that it is of very little use, no steamboat can get near it. I think it would not cost much to do sufficient dredging to let a steamboat in. I would like to say that the Gypsum Company has been in operation for years, they are shipping hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of gypsum down that lake, and they are compelled now, for the want, of a wharf, to take it right down to the bottom of Lake Manitoba and up the Westbourne river, and it is very difficult to get up that river, and very expensive. I am satisfied if the minister understood the situation he would complete that dock.
It is a curious thing that none of these interests have communicated with me on the subject at all.
What would it cost to finish that in proper shape?
I have not that information, but I would be glad to get it.

Will the minister send his engineer up there and get estimates, provided he is not prepared to take the word of the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) and myself with regard to the usefulness of it? Will the minister even go that far, and ascertain what is required to be done, and about what will be the cost?
I shall be glad to look into the matter further, and to get a report from the engineer, Mr. Dufresne, who I presume is familiar with all the facts.
Would you not have information as to the cost in the department?
We no doubt have the original scheme as outlined, but I would not have a report as to the present condition.

There is a matter I wish to bring up though it does not come under this item, but under the next one. There is another piece of work the government have been doing in the constituency of Portage La Prairie, adjacent to the constituency of Macdonald; that is on the Assi-niboine river. Could the minister give me any information as to the condition of that work? It is with reference to straightening out the river in order to let the water run a little more freely, and prevent the flooding of some land.
I would like very much if my hon. friend would intimate to me

beforehand what information he wants on any particular item. I have not got the papers here to-night, or any notes in connection with any work except those that are actually in these estimates. I could not give my hon. friend the information which he asks for. All I know is that the work was reported as being very useful, but just in what stage it is I am not prepared to say.

I think it is pretty well completed. I have a return here that I moved for last session, in reference to this piece of work. This piece of work, like other work in that district, has occasioned a great deal of dissatisfaction. There is quite a large return here, and it is really laughable to read some of the communications. I find that some keen politicians were mixed up in it in the election of 1908. They even went so far as to dip down into their own pockets and pay the necessary money in order to keep the work going without creating dissatisfaction until the election was over. That is the position of affairs. They went on and completed this work on a piece of land before they even had a title to it. Now the Minister of Public Works cannot get away from this particular piece of work, he was minister, I believe, at the time. I think it is nearly completed now. But there are some letters here that would really make a person laugh to read them, from men who were concerned, Mr. Macpherson, a lawyer from Portage la Prairie, and even the outside leader of the opposition in Manitoba, Mr. Edward Brown, who was very active in it, and guaranteed the payment to a certain Mr. Armstrong for certain lands. But before he got through with the government, they wrote even to the Minister of Public Works very strong letters, that would indicate they were not very well satisfied with the way in which the government had treated them. I do not know what understanding there may have been between the government and these particular persons. But Mr. Macpherson had to write a good many letters, and write some rather plain letters, before he got his money back that he had put in it, and also certain other bills paid. The minister apparently does not know in what condition the work is in, and I would suggest that he let this item stand until he arms himself with the necessary information.

Much as I would like to oblige my hon friend, he must see how unreasonable it would be to let these items for the coming year all stand over until I can get some information of a work that was done upwards of a year ago, and with regard to which he can get the fullest information before the Public Accounts Committee
I moved for this return on the 22nd of April last year, and only got it a few days ago.

My hon. friend does not understand. He seems to think it has been done. As far as I know, he regards that as being satisfactory. But what my hon. friend wants to do is to indulge his curiosity in regard to what he says took place between some of the people engaged on the work. I must urge that this item of harbours, rivers and bridges should not be allowed to stand over. We will come later on to a dredging vote. Probably next week there will be some further items in public works, and I shall be glad to get the information for my hon. friend, but I trust he will not urge that these important items should stand over. We want to get along as rapidly as we can. I hope to get as far as the British Columbia items to-night, and I hope my hon. friend will not endeavour to delay these items.

I do not wish to retard the progress of this House a moment. I have sat in this committee night after night when the minister had his estimates before the committee, waiting for an opportunity to bring up one or two little things regarding Manitoba, and I do not think he can accuse me of entering into any discussion for the purpose of delaying the House. But I do not propose to allow the minister to sit down and say that I have brought these items up simply as a matter of curiosity.
I think this committee is entitled to know the way in which this government have undertaken to do certain public works, and that they have undertaken to do this piece of work on land for which they had not the title. I do not think that is conducting public business on a very good principle. This work was done on property before they had the title. The minister cannot get away from that.
The title is in the Crown.
It is now; it was not when this work was going on.

Do I understand the
minister to say that we can discuss any question relating to Manitoba?
At any time.
Can we get anything more definite than this statement of ' harbours, rivers and bridges '?

Perhaps I can answer my hon. friend's question best by showing him what was expended last year. Last-year, we only spent $2,654, but the resident-engineer thinks that, taking all the different works together, we ought to take a vote of $8,000. We may not spend the whole
of it; we may not spend more than two-thirds of it.
Just for repairs?

Just for general repairs and work which may spring up during the fiscal year for which we have no other provision.
Lake Winnipeg-wharfs, $10,000. .

This is an amount which we are taking to provide for what we think possibly may be some wharf accommodation required on Lake Winnipeg in view of the improvements which have just been completed at St. Andrew's rapids, and which will enable steamers to leave the city of Winnipeg, pass down te Red River and to the foot of Lake Winnipeg. We believe that there will be considerable traffic developed, and we think that necessarily it will have to be provided, for by thej building of one -or two wharfs which would probably serve as breakwaters as well. There should be at the northern part of the lake a breakwater, and we -may utilize that as a wharf as well.
Has the minister any idea where any of these wharfs should be built?
We have not decided at what places, because it is a new business that is going to be opened up.

I understand. I would like to say that at Gimli there is already a government wharf with an L built across. We hope that the government will extend that L for the purpose of making a harbour there. It is now the terminus of the Canadian Pacific railway on Lake Winnipeg and it is a very important place. I do not know whether the government have a petition or not, but I think that a petition from Gimli was prepared asking for the extension of this wharf, 120 or 150 feet.
They are asking for 100 feet.	*

That is a very important matter, and I would like to impress upon the minister the necessity of doing the work. All the boats that ply from Selkirk to the head of Lake Winnipeg pass this place. It is a very shallow lake, storms come up very rapidly, and the waves get very ugly there. There is no way of getting into Gimli when there is a heavy sea on at the present time, and if this 100 feet were built and a little dredging done it would make a first-class harbour for any boat on the lake, and it would be a great benefit to the people of Gimli, to the steamboat owners and t-o everybody wh-o is doing business on that lake. I would, therefore, urge the minister to -provide a sum to extend the wharf at this point this year.

We have been already urged to make an extension of the wharf at Gimli, and the matter is under consideration. It will be quite possible to use part of this vote for this purpose. We intend to have a pretty careful survey of the harbours of Lake Winnipeg made with the view of expending any money on wharfs at points where it would be of the greatest advantage, always keeping in mind the importance of having some harbours of refuge which are essential to the preservation of life and the safety of shipping. As my hon. friend knows, storms arise very quickly on that lake, and it is essential to the safety of shipping that there should be some harbours of refuge at different points on the lake.

The building "of these wharfs on Lake Winnipeg, the deepening of _ the river at the mouth and the construction of the St. Andrew's rapids all point to the fact that the destination of the trade which is expected to be developed will be the city of Winnipeg. If it is to be the destination of that trade we certain want wharfs. In the olden times when the river was navigated by the old Eed Eiver steamers with flat bottoms and stern wheels, any part of the bank was a wharf. They simply ran the prow of the boat upon the prairie and loaded or unloaded. But, if Lake Winnipeg is to be navigated, it will be by lake steamers which will come up through the lake and the Eed. river, and we will want a wharf at Winnipeg; otherwise there will be great inconvenience to transportation. There is expected to be a large trade in stone, timber and cordwood, and unless there are facilities for unloading there will be great inconvenience. Just in connection with this I would like to mention that now would be the time to procure a site, and now would be the time to lay out a plan for the wharf, because property along that river is being very rapidly acquired, a great deal of it by the railway companies. The minister ought not to lose sight of that.
With reference to the bridge over the St. Andrews dam-
We are going to build that bridge.
That is just what I want to know.
Yes.
Then I will not discuss it. I am very glad that the minister has seen the necessity of doing that work.
Does the minister mean that he is going to build the approaches?
The approaches to the bridge.
The intention is to build the approaches?

The intention is to complete this work by building the approaches. The bridge is designed as a service bridge in connection with the dam, and also for a highway bridge. I just want to say, I have to say it now in the absence of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), that I was greatly surprised at the statement he made here as to the uselessness of that work at St. Andrews rapids, and I was more surprised that hon. gentlemen from Manitoba who are familiar with the facts, and know the vast public importance of this work should allow these remarks to pass unnoticed. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) stated it was a waste of public money, that he had been down to see it, that it was a splendid piece of work which was entirely unnecessary, and would not serve any good purpose. That is the effect of what the hon. member for North Toronto said.

I think the minister is doing the hon. member (Mr. Foster) an injustice. I understood him to say that owing to the elevation of that work, although it is a good piece of work, it would be of no value unless approaches were built.

No, the hon. member (Mr. Foster) was speaking of the whole work as being away beyond the necessity of the times, and as being an extravagance and a waste of public money. I desire to say that in my judgment there is no more useful work in Canada than that lock and dam in St. Andrews rapids. There is no work that is more likely to lead in the near future to a large traffic. We have designed the bridge as a highway bridge, and a service bridge. The extra expenditure to make it a highway bridge is not very great, and we purpose proceeding during the coming season with the building of the approaches. I visited this work, and I met there the representatives of the municipalities, and I told them I would take their request into my careful consideration. I have much pleasure in announcing for the information of our friends from that portion of Manitoba which is more particularly interested in this work, that during the coming season we will build the approaches to the bridge so that the people on both sides may have the accommodation.

The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) does not need any one to defend him in this House, but he is not here to defend himself, and while I think the minister does not want to be unfair to the hon. member (Mr. Foster), yet the minister made a mistake when he said that the hon. member for North Toronto had declared the work to be useless.
He made a big mistake.

I was present with the hon. member (Mr. Foster) when he investigated this work, and what he did say was that he considered the expenditure altogether too large for the requirements of the place. As the representative of that constituency I am not prepared to say that the hon. member (Mr. Foster) was not right. The government has spent a large sum of money there, and they have certainly done an excellent piece of work, and I must give the department credit for having erected one of the best steel structures of that kind on this continent.
Hear, hear.

Whether that large expenditure is warranted at the present time I am not prepared to say, but at all events, what the hon. member for North Toronto argued was that the putting of the passenger bridge on top of the work required for the steel girders to allow the ice to pass had occasioned an increased expenditure of something like $200,000.
The increase would not be $20,000.
I have to take the word of the minister, but against it I have the word of the engineer in charge of the bridge at the time whom I asked what the extra cost of providing for the passenger bridge was-

My hon. friend will pardon me. The hon. member for North Toronto was simply speaking of the bridge that was there; he was not speaking of the approaches, and he said we had spent $200, 000 beyond what it would have been necessary to spend if we had not provided that portion of it for a highway bridge, and he said that money was wasted. As to that he is all wrong; my engineer informs me that $20,000 will be the extra cost.
Had the minister maintained his position of last session that he would not build the approaches-
I did not say I would [DOT] not.
It was pretty near that.
Oh, no.
If the minister had not built the approaches then the member for North Toronto would be right.
I have been up there since, you know, and I have seen the place.

When the member for North Toronto criticised that work he stated that it was an excellent piece of work, but at the same time he did not feel that the large expenditure was justified at the present -time. The hon. member (Mr. Foster) pointed out with reference to the lock, and I think he was right in that, that if the traffic from Lake Winnipeg and the north is going to be anything as- great as that heavy expenditure would indicate, then the lock is surely too small, because at the present time it will not tak-e an ordinary lake barge and a tug at the same time, it is only possible to take one barge through the lock by the old style of towing. Probably that is one of the things the attention of the hon. member (Mr. Foster) was drawn to when he was on the ground, and he realized that a larger lock should be provided in view of the great expenditure. I think the minister told me lasit year that the work would cost $1,500,000.
Not so much, about $1,250,000.

I will not criticise this work further. I congratulate the minister that at last he has seen eye to eye with myself as to the absolute necessity of completing that work. It would have been folly to allow that -work to stand in the position it was in last year because it was useless for a passenger bridge as no one could get near it. I am glad the minister has made up his imind to complete it.
Red River projection-new entrance to channel at its mouth, $10,000.
What does the minister intend to do at the mouth of the river?	*

We are to build protecting jetties to prevent the filling of the new channel at the mouth of the river. These jetties are to be respectively 400 feet and 300 feet long, pile work. A new channel 4,000 feeit long and about a hundred feet wide, 4 feet 5 inches deep at low water and 9 feet 5 inches deep at high water, has been dredged at the bar, and we propose, by means of these protection jetties, to keep the current in that channel.

That is a work which is very much needed, and I am glad the department is taking that way of making the channel. Thousands of dollars have

been wasted at the mouth of the river, and the method which the government is adopting wall I hope make a permanent channel.
Winnipeg Beach harbour-protection pier on Lake Winnipeg, $10,000.
This is a very necessary work, and we propose going on with it this year.	.

I may say that this is a very necessary work. I urged this on the hon. minister last year as strongly as I could. He stated that the finances of the country did not then warrant him in going on with the work, but I am glad that he has provided for it this year. I have in my hand a petition from the residents of Winnipeg Beach, addressed to the ministgr, and signed by the mayor of the village, W. J. Woods, by counsellors A. C. Dukes, J. Stacey, Wm. J. Howes, and by the secretary, J. D. Forster, praying that this work be commenced immediately and be completed as soon as possible. They point out the absolute necessity of commencing the work before the ice goes away, if the minister has any intention of building it this spring, as I hope he has, because a great deal of the piling can be done on the ice, which could not be done afterwards, except at much greater expense.

I may say that I have seen the locality and recognize the very great importance of this work, in the way of providing a suitable breakwater and harbour of refuge at this point on Lake Winnipeg. We are endeavouring to expedite the work as much as possible. We are taking all the preliminary steps in the hope that by next week we shall probably be able to call for tenders, so that the moment the Appropriation Act passes a contract can be entered into. In the meantime it will be intimated to the parties who are the lowest tenderers, so that they can get the timber out before the ice leaves. Now, let me call the attention of the .committee to the remarks of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) on the subject of the dam and lock at St. Andrews. It was a matter of surprise to me that my hon. friends from Manitoba should have let those remarks pass without correcting the hon. gentleman. I think common fair play to the Department of Public Works and to the government should have induced the hon. gentlemen who are so zealous for this work and know its importance to correct the hon. member for North Toronto. This is what the hon. gentleman is reported to have said, at page 1498 of 'Hansard.'
What was being debated at that time?

It was the Budget. Referring to St. Andrews lock, the hon. member for North Toronto said:
Mr. BRADBURY
Whilst in the west, I took an automobile trip down the Red river to see a very notable, noted, or notorious work, called the St. Andrew's lock. There you have a very fine work. The total cost of it, I believe, is to be over $600,000.
A million and a half.
Six hundred thousand dollars has been spent now.
Over a million.
It is worse than I thought it was. Supposing we put it at a million or a million and a quarter. Has the Prime Minister ever seen it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have not had that privilege.'
Has the Prime Minister ever inquired into it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

That is a very weak reply. The Prime Minister is head trustee for the people of Canada. Will he now justify his conduct as head trustee for the people of Canada in sinking a million and a quarter of money in the St. Andrew's locks? Of that amount, $200,000 is for a highway bridge, for which no vote was ever taken, and that bridge lies there in its naked steel splendour, thirty-five or forty feet up in air from the road on either side.
Let me pause to remark that that bridge is essentially and primarily a service bridge for the purpose of operating these curtains in connection with the dam, and the amount spent to date on making that service bridge a highway bridge, which was also to be used as a highway- bridge, was somewhere between $20,000 and $30,000 instead of $200,000 as stated by the hon. member for North Toronto. Then he proceeds :
I want to ask the Prime Minister, as head trustee for the people of Canada, to tell me to-night if he can get any three business men in the city of Winnipeg to put within his hand any justification, on the traffic that exists at present or on the business which may be expected in the near future, for the ex- ' penditure of a million and a quarter of money on that work? It is one of the finest pieces of concrete masonry and steel I ever saw; but where is the business to come from ? It is an absolute waste of public money at the present time. Was that brilliant work, when the head trustee himself does not know a thing about it? Who does know? Somebody; and somebody ought to have told it.
If my hon. friend thought then, as he thinks to-night, that this was a most useful public work, and that it opened up possibilities for the development of traffic in stone, timber, cordwood and other resources, which will no doubt be developed in the future along the shores of that great lake, which is larger than Lake Ontario, surely it was his duty to have risen in the House and told the hon. member for North Toronto and the people of Canada that he was entirely mistaken in charging the government with building a public work for which there would be no business, and

which, therefore, was an absolute waste of public money. I desire to say that I have carefully inquired into the matter, and I do believe that the construction of that lock and dam at St. Andrews rapids is going to be the means of opening up between points on Lake Winnipeg and the city of Winnipeg a traffic which will grow to very large dimensions; and a man does not need to have a very prophetic vision to be able to look forward to the not distant future when, by the construction of a few locks near the mouth of the Saskatchewan, we can hatve steamboat accommodation all the way from Winnipeg to within a comparatively short distance of the foothills of the Eocky mountains, about 100 miles west of Edmonton, and this dam at St. Andrews rapids is the first link in this great chain of inland transportation.

I am not going to dispute what the hon. gentleman says as regards the importance of this work. But I do not think it is altogether fair to the hon. member for North Toronto. He seeks to convey to this committee and to the country that the hon. member for North Toronto condemned the work in its entirety. This would not be fair or correct.
If language means anything, he did.

I differ with the hon. gentleman. What the hon. member for North Toronto said was that a million and a quarter was a larger amount of money than was justified under the circumstances. This work has a history which the hon. minister does not perhaps know; but we who have lived in that country, some twenty-five years know that government after government has been approached to build this great work. I remember that when the Hon. McKenzie Bowell, who was then premier of this Dominion, was in Winnipeg, he met the board of trade of that city at the city hall, and after listening to their representations, he told them that if they could show him anything to justify the expenditure, he would make it. At that time the engineers of the government estimated the cost at half a million dollars, but it has cost instead $1,500,000 or very close to that amount. I am not prepared to admit that such a large expenditure was absolutely necessary to create the dam and the dock at St. Andrews rapidf but the work erected there is a magnificent piece of work and a credit to the government that did it. I believe, however, that we could have built a piece of work there, which would have answered the purpose just as well for perhaps one half the expenditure the government have made. That, I think, was the position which the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) took.
You could hardly get that system of curtains for the amount you mention.
The minister will admit that this is the only system of curtains on this continent.
Quite so, and this is the only work of that character on this continent.
I do not think so You will find other rivers that have a dam and a lock built along these lines.
Eunning from south to north ?
I do not know.
That is just where the difference is.

I am quite satisfied that a work could have been built there which would have suited the purpose just as well for much less money. Fifteen yearn ago we had as resident engineer in Winnipeg, one of the brightest engineers the department has ever had, and he never proposed any such work as this. There can be no question that we could have built a work which would have answered the purpose just as well, without these steel curtains. At the same time, now that the work is completed, I am not going to criticise it; but when the hon. member for North Toronto spoke, what he deprecated was the very large expenditure in excess of what he thought was justified under the circumstances. He was not condemning the work itself or a proper expenditure. Had he done so, I would have expressed my dissent.
I understood the hon. minister to say that work was contracted for, involving an expenditure of about $200,000, before there was any item in the estimates.
No. That is what the hon. member for North Toronto said. He said that $200,000 had been expended without any vote, but that statement lacked the essential element of truth.

I think we might now leave this. This bridge has been built, the money has been spent, the work is there, we have had the opinion of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), and we now have the opinion of the minister, and I certainly sympathize with the minister and hope that every prophecy he has made will be realized. In connection with the other item, the building of this pier at Winnipeg beach, that is a work in which the people of Winnipeg are deeply interested. That beach has been much improved by the Canadian Pacific railway. It is within about 40 miles of the

city, and is one of the outing places for its population of 170,000. By furnishing fast trains and giving good accommodation, the Canadian Pacific railway has given the people of Winnipeg the opportunity of enjoying an outing at that beach for the day or the week's end. A large amount of pleasure craft have their headquarters there, but these boats run the risk of being destroyed by every storm that blows. During Christmas time I was approached by many people who represented to me the crying need for the construction of a pier at that beach, and they want it begun now so that they may enjoy the benefit of it this summer. Now that the river has been dredged, there is water communication between Winnipeg and that beach, but no valuahle boat can be left there over night for lack of this protection. Hundreds' of people have cottages and live there during the summer months, as it is convenient for business men who can leave there in the morning and be in town in time for their work. It is really the only summer resort near Winnipeg where people can have their summer homes, and at the same time attend daily to their business. All classes of citizens have been urging me to use my best endeavours to have the minister go on with that work with all the expedition possible, but I doubt very much if the sum of $10,000 will be adequate.
It will take something more than that, but w i intend to proceed as rapidly as possible with it. It will take about $16,000 to finish it.

I want to draw the
attention of the minister to the fact that at Hecla island, or Big island, on Lake Winnipeg, there are about 50 or 60 settlers. It is an old settled district. All the steamers coming to or going from the north pass by this island, and a great many stop there to take on wood. A wharf of some kind should be built at that place, and I would urge the hon. minister to investigate it this summer, and have his [DOT]engineers select a site for a wharf there. I notice in the estimates quite a number of wharfs provided in the eastern provinces, and I do not think I am asking too much when I urge on the minister to provide a wharf at this island. It would not cost more than $5,000 or $6,000 and will be a great accommodation to steamboats and people who have no wav of gst-ting from the island except by boat. There is a large quantity of wood there, which has now to be shipped under great difficulties, besides agricultural products.

My object in providing this vote was to do these very things. It is to provide that, after careful examination, we may give wharf accommodation where needed. The representation of my Mr. A. HAGGART.
hon. friend regarding Hecla island will have my most serious consideration.

With regard to the appropriations for 1910-11, I would like to ask the minister what has happened the yearly appropriation I have seen in the estimates during the last five or six years for the lowering of Lake Dauphin and taking care of the silt at the mouth of the Mossv river? Is there any special reason why these works have been, eliminated?

This work, if it be useful work, of course the government will look into carefully. It can be done out of the general dredging vote with our own dredging plant, and we do not require a.special appropriation for it.

The dredging at the mouth of the Mossy river was done in a very inadequate way, those operating the dredge knew nothing about their business, they took up the mud from one side of the boat and dumped it on the other, and the northeast wind sent the sand back into the old channel. If the dredging is not done this summer, it would be impossible for boats to get into the mouth of the river.
I am going to have it looked into. I have not been satisfied "with the way that work has been proceeding, and I want to see if we cannot have it go along more satisfactorily.

Thank you.
Harbours and rivers, Saskatchewan and Alberta-Athabaska riier-removal of boulders and deepening channel through sand and gravel bars, $10,000.

This is to do work urgently required to improve the navigation of the Athabaska river. There is a gerat deal of settlement going on north of Edmonton and we have as rapidly as possible to make provision for the people. The only way to get to remote districts is by the river. Some have motor boats, some small steamers, and some York boats and we are endeavouring to remove the boulders, etc., as fast as we can. The same remarks apply to the items for the Lesser Slave lake and the North Saskatchewan river.
Last Mountain lake-improvement of navigable route, $24,000.
Would the minister give some information in regard to this work, the length of the navigable route, the amount of traffic, etc.?

There is a great deal of settlement upon both sides of Last Mountain lake. A steamboat has been put in operation on the lake and is doing a very considerable, business. This work is to make the outlet and the mouth of the lake navigable. We have been dredging at the

entrance right into the lake so that a small steamer will be able to leave the railway at Craven and go up into the lake. The idea is that lumber and other supplies can be taken up to the settlers by water and grain can be brought down. Last Mountain lake is the one great sheet ol water in the western country west ol the Manitoba lakes. It is a beautiful sheet of water and there are a number of fine harbours on it. It is rapidly becoming a very favourite summer resort for the people of Regina. There is excellent fishing and, better than all, both sides of the lake for many miles back are settled by a very large number of industrious and thrifty settlers who have been very prosperous and who have improved the country in a few years.
What is the actual distance of navigation being opened up, what has it cost and what is it likely to cost before it is completed?

From Craven to the head of the lake, I would think would be about 60 miles of navigable water. I shall be able to give my hon. friend the details of the expenditure at a later date. I have not a memorandum of them here. We built a small dredge and a tug and have been dredging there. There will also be land damages on account of flooding.
What is the area of land damaged?

By building a dam at Craven in order to preserve the water in Last Mountain lake at normal level a considerable area of land below the foot of the lake and in the valley of the outlet was flooded, and we expropriated quite a quantity of land, I think about 1,800 acres, thinking it better to. expropriate the land than to pay damages. The Exchequer Court allowed $25 an acre. I believe that by utilizing the dredge to make a dyke along the foot of the lake and at the outlet we will be able to shut out the water and the land in a few years will be worth as much as we paid for it.
North Saskatchewan river-wing dams for improvement of navigable channel from Edmonton to Lake Winnipeg, $25,000.
What does this improvement consist of?

Building wing dams for the purpose of confining the channel at certain points within narrow limits, in order to increase the depth of water. There are a number of places where navigation can be greatly improved in this way. I believe we can get, at a moderate expenditure, very good navigation from the head of Cedar lake, at all events, right through to a point west of Edmonton, without build 136
ing any locks. Down the river below Cedar lake some locks will be necessary to make navigation reasonably good.
Will the minister say what is the nature of navigation on the Saskatchewan, and what trade is being done there?

At present there are quite a number of steamers operating at different points, but there is no through traffic from Edmonton to Winnipeg. There are steamers between different points. At Prince Albert there are a number of small vessels, and at Edmonton also. There is a good deal of settlement springing up along the bank^ of the Saskatchewan, and people living at Prince Albert and other points up and down the river, are of the opinion that it is desirable to preserve and improve gradually the navigation of the river. It is felt that it will be a most desirable means of bringing heavy freight from the prairie country, from the towns along the Saskatchewan, and from the farms in the vicinity, freight such as grain, coal and lumber down the Saskatchewan, to go either over the Hudson Bay railway to Hudson bay and thence to Europe, or to the city of Winnipeg. Coal would only be brought to Winnipeg, but lumber might be shipped over the Hudson Bay railway. If it were brought down by water, it could take the Hudson Bay railway at Le Pas and could thence be shipped to Europe. Of course it is impossible to tell the extent to which development will take place. But I do think that our western country is very fortunate in having such a vast system of inland navigation as we have on both branches of the Saskatchewan, and along the tributary streams such as the Carrot river. The main river has been more or less explored from time to time. During the past season, I directed an exploring party to go from the mouth of the river up as far as Le Pas where the Hudson Bay railway will start. A very valuable report has been made, and the engineers report that it will be practicable to give nine feet of navigation at low Water to the head of Cedar lake, and in that way lake vessels navigating Lake Winnipeg could go up the Saskatchewan river to the head of Cedar lake, and from Cedar lake on to a point probably 100 miles west of Edmonton. Navigation would be suitable in the dry season only for light vessels drawing three or four feet of water; but that is the class of vessels which are largely used in navigating the waters of the western rivers in the United States, such as the Missouri, the Ohio, and ports of the Mississippi. My hon. friend probably knows about the South Saskatchewan. I know there are steamers, tug boats and other vessels plying upon that river. Of course the build-



ing of railways has done away to a large extent with the navigation that formerly was done on the Saskatchewan river. But as the country settles up, I think the time will soon come when people will look to water transportation as the chief means of getting heavy produce carried to market. Navigable rivers will prove valuable to regulate railway rates; and if there is one thing more than another I would like to say to the people of that western country, it is to preserve at all hazards the navigation of these rivers, not to allow any obstruction in them in the shape of building fixed bridges, or otherwise, but rather to induce the government to keep on improving and preserving navigation, because it will be found of incalculable value as the country develops in the future.

I am aware that there has been some navigation on the Saskatchewan river for 30 years back. But the minister has not told us definitely to what extent navigation is carried on there at the present time. I would like to know, for instance, if there are any steamers running regular trips on schedule time from Edmonton east as far as Prince Albert, or for what distance, or are they only used as ferry boats? Is there any freight at the present time carried up and down the Saskatchewan river?	,
I could not say that.

I think I could give some information to my hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Herron). There was considerable boat traffic on that river until the Canadian Northern was built two years ago. There is no boat running regularly between Prince Albert and Edmonton, hut there is some boats running from Edmonton taking on freight to Battleford, and it is also used for the shipment of coal. The improvement of this river is much needed. Along the banks of the Saskatchewan river there are many outcroppings of coal, sometimes a hundred feet or 150 feet below the level, and it costs more to raise the coal up and draw it to the railway than it is worth. If the river was made navigable, it would afford a cheaper means of transporting coal than is now available, and would give an opportunity to ship coal to Battleford and Prince Albert. There is no railroad north of the Saskatchewan river, but there are large farming settlements, cattle and grain, and could be better shipped by boat than by rail. I think that if some of the boulders were removed from the river we would see regular boats running during the summer months between Edmonton and Prince Albert. They would carry a good deal of freight, and I think all the coal on the Saskatchewan might be carried that way.

I hope the minister will have his department prepare some comprehensive plan for the development of the water routes in that country. He has spoken about the North Saskatchewan. It is _ desirable, in making expenditures of this kind, that they shall all form a link in the final result that he expects _ to reach. Water transportation in America has not been satisfactory. The hon. gentleman was speaking, a few moments ago, about the Missouri. I remember when the upper reaches of the Missouri were crowded with steamers, - and there are none there to-day. The railroads appear to have been shoving these waterways out of business. I do not hold that that is desirable. I think that expenditures of this character should be in line with a common policy and that a proper engineering force should be put to work along our western streams and a thorough investigation made so that every dollar we spend will be leading towards the perfected plan of final developments.

That comes under the next item for surveys of rapids, &c., on the North and South Saskatchewan river, and other navigable streams.
Northwest Territories-harbours, river and bridge work-general repairs and improvements, $5,000.

This is for work in the Northwest territories outside of the provinces.
British Columbia - Athalmer - Columbia river-wharf, $1,500.	'

This is to provide for the construction of a small wharf at Athalmer, asked for by a petition of the residents. This will complete the work.
Bamfield-west shore of Vancouver Island, $5,000.
Mr., PUGSLEY. This is for the renewal and enlargement of the existing wharf at Bamfield. It is asked for by the superintendent of the cable station and others.
Campbell river-improvements and wharf, $5,000.
This is requested by the resident engineer, and it is for repairs to Campbell river wharf.
What is the work that is going to be done?

The wharf is to be renewed. It has been very severely damaged by the teredo. It is useless to renew it without protecting the piles. The engineer recommends that a Gold teredo proof pile should be used in the renewals as it will last ten or fifteen years and will cost $5,000. '

I notice that some of I the wharfs being built in the province of

Quebec, that we were discussing this afternoon, were apparently being built of concrete, and that the cost was more or less estimated by the cubic contents, showing that work of a practically permanent nature was being constructed. I think it is almost conceded that no piles in the waters of the Pacific coast will stand the attacks of the teredo for many more than a feiy years. Has the minister ever considered the idea of making these wharfs of a permanent nature by putting in concrete or (something that will do away with the necessity of this constant renewal?
To build piers of concrete in British Columbia at the present time would be pretty expensive. I do not know that there are any cement works out there.
I can give the minister some information as to that. There is no trouble about getting cement. You can get a very good quality of cement on Vancouver island.
Is it manufactured there?
Yes, at one of the best plants in the country.
It is certainly worthy of considering as to whether or not it would be better, as far as possible to build of concrete in places where the teredo is very destructive.
That is everywhere.

It seems that it is almost everywhere on the coast except in the Fraser river where you have fresh water. The chief engineer of the department informs me that there is a timber called turpentine timber which is got in Australia-The Canadian Pacific railway are beginning to use it-which is said to resist the ravages of the teredo, and it may be that we will find it of advantage to use it and that it will be cheaper than concrete. It is supposed that it will last, as against the teredo, for forty or fifty years.
Columbia river-improvements, $14,500.
This is for general improvement upon the Columbia river.
Where?
At Revelstoke, above Golden and at the Arrow lake wharf. These are three which we are urgently asked to attend to.
Are any of the works which are to be constructed at Revelstoke in the nature of protecting the bank against erosion?
No.

I understand that representations have been made along this 136J
