line by the provincial government on account of this being a navigable stream. I would like to know if the minister has taken into consideration the desirability of doing that work?

Part of this money will be used for protecting the works there that we have already contributed to, but we have not- in contemplation the undertaking of any new work of this nature upon the Columbia river at the present time. I have been communicated with by the British Columbia government asking me to pay half of a certain work that they are carrying on. I have not felt it advisable to accede to their request.

We have to-day voted numerous items for the protection of the banks of the St. Lawrence and other rivers in the east. I would like to know if there is any reason why this government should not undertake the protection of the banks of navigable rivers in the province of British Columbia in the same way as they do in the east?

We are finishing up some works of this character in the east, which were undertaken some time ago, the same as we have done work in British Columbia and in other provinces, but, for reasons which I stated upon another occasion, I do not feel that we could, as a general rule, engage in work of this character. I do not feel that we could recognize that this is an obligation which rests upon the federal government. There may be circumstances under which we will continue to do it. There may be cases in which the work is of such great magnitude that it would not be reasonable to ask the province to do it entirely. In those cases we may perhaps fairly assume a part of the burden, but to say that we are bound, as a matter of duty and obligation simply because a river is navigable, as a federal government, to do the work of protecting the banks is to put forth a proposition which I deny in toto. I say that there is no obligation of that character resting upon the federal government. It will not do for the provincial authorities or the municipal authorities to attempt to throw that work on to the federal government, and to say this is work which it is your duty to attend to, simply because a river' ot a lake that is washing away the shores is navigable water. There are cases where we have done it. We have assisted the local government in British Columbia, but it does not follow that because we have given them some assistance we are going to assist them in every work of this character that they undertake. If we did that we would be called upon to do work of this character on the McLeod river, the Saskatchewan, the St. Lawrence, the Lievre

and hundreds of other lakes and rivers of Canada. There is another reason. We are already doing work on the Columbia river for which we are asking an appropriation of $14,500, and we are dealing as liberally as the funds at our disposal will enable us to do to improve the navigation of these rivers. We are going to clear out the debris in the steamboat channels for the purpose of assisting navigation. We are doing a great deal of work in various sections of British Columbia along these lines. I cannot undertake that as a matter of federal obligation we would protect the banks of all rivers simply because they happen to be navigable.
The minister has got heated over this matter.
Not at all.

I simply asked the minister whether he was going to do this work, and if not, whether he thought there was any distinction between the treatment accorded to British Columbia and the treatment accorded to the province of Quebec. I merely mentioned the province of Quebec in the comparison for the reason that we have had, to-day, several appropriations for work of a similar character in that province. I would like to know from the minister if we are to take it that it is not the policy of the government to do this kind of work in any of the provinces in 'the future unless special circumstances arise.

There is one thing the hon. gentleman seems to desire to forget, and that is that if he looks to the protection work that has been done in the different provinces in recent years, I venture to say that as much or more has been done in British Columbia as m any other province of Canada. But the hon. gentleman does not recognize that, and he seems to be wanting all the time to put forward the allegation that we are discriminating against British Columbia.
So you are.
As a matter of fact, we have done more of this kind of work in British Columbia than in any other province in Canada.
I would like to ask the supporters of the government from British Columbia if they consider that the province of British Columbia has been as fairly treated as have the other provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is another question.

That is a question which neither the hon. member for Nanaimo nor the Minister of Inland Revenue will venture to answer to-night.
Mr -PUGSLEY.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not the question before the committee.
It is a great pity to raise these sectional questions.

The question before the committee is not a sectional question; it is a question of honour between the Dominion of Canada and the province of British Columbia, which makes it far more than a sectional question. We have a solemn agreement with the Dominion of Canada and that agreement has been violated in several respects. We have a solemn agreement providing that the federal government shall carry on in British Columbia all classes of works which it carries on in the other provinces of Canada. That is the principle for which the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Barnard) has been contending to-night. It is not a matter of expediency, it is not a matter of policy on the part of the government, it is a matter of whether or not they intend to break faith with British Columbia. The minister and his colleagues recognize that it is a very difficult thing indeed for a province to compel the federal administration to keep faith in a matter of this kind, but there is such a thing as honour left in this country, and we have put it forward as a matter of honour time after time, that they have made a contract with us to do these works, and that they are doing them for other provinces as I showed this afternoon in regard to the province of Quebec when I read item after item-and I mentioned Quebec merely because the items for that province were before the House when the matter came up-item after item appearing in the estimates for all sorts of protection works in that province. I invited the intention of the Minister of Public Works to that fact in view of this discussion this afternoon. Now I would like to ask the minister whether he repudiates this contract with British Columbia or whether he thinks this government should carry it out in the spirit in which it was made?

If the hon. gentleman asks me the question I would say that so far as this government is aware it is carrying out in the most absolute, good faith every obligation to British Columbia. It does not follow that because we build a wharf in one province we have got to build a wharf in British Columbia whether it is required or not.
That is not the question.

We are carrying on all classes of work in British Columbia just the same as in the other sections of Canada. The Dominion is giving subsidies for railways in British Columbia just as

in other sections of the country; it is building wharfs in British Columbia, and it is doing dredging work in British Columbia just the same as in any other section of Canada.
Not the same.

The point beforj the committee is: Will the government continue to erect protection works in British Columbia or will it follow out the policy of refusing to do so, which has been indicated by the Minister of Public Works?
Our policy in regard to protection works will be the same in British Columbia as in every other province of Canada.

The Minister of Public Works told us he was doing dredging work in British Columbia the same as in other provinces. I have not been in this House very long, but I have had two opportunities of showing the minister that the tonnage of the ports of British Columbia exceeds the tonnage of these pet ports of his in the maritime provinces very largely indeed. And I have also told him that the province of British Columbia in connection with these harbour works and harbour and dredging appropriations gets about 20 per cent in proportion of the appropriations that the other provinces get.
I have pointed out that the province of British Columbia is to-dav crying out for these public works and it is crying to deaf ears.

The Minister of Public Works is seeking shelter in his own ignorance when he says he ' is not aware,' and perhaps it is my duty to put him wise to the facts. The fact is that this government is taking three times as much per head of the population from the people of British Columbia as it is taking out of the people of the other parts of the Dominion, and this government is spending in public works in British Columbia about one-fifth as much per head of the population as it is spending in the other parts of Canada. In other words, this government is discriminating against British Columbia about eight times. Where there should be an exact equality, where on every principle of honour there should be an exact equality, there is a difference of about eight to one against British Columbia. Now, the minister has sheltered himself twice under the statement that he is unaware of the facts, and I venture to say on the floor of this House that I am stating the facts when I give these figures.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
And I venture to state that my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Cowan) is not stating the facts with regard to the proportion of expenditure in
British Columbia as compared with the other provinces in the Dominion. My hon. friend, I believe, claims to be the father of the famous better terms proposition of the British Columbia government, and the fallacy of the figures presented in the tabulated statement he has caused to be prepared was absolutely proven by the return brought down to this House a few years ago.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman could show where that fallacy is?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: It is shown in the return brought down to which I have referred. The hon. member is making general statements to the House and is not producing any proof whatever to substantiate what he says. He simply says that the appropriations for expenditure in British Columbia are as one to eight in the rest of the Dominion, and he claims that the contribution to the revenue by the province of British Columbia is much larger than the contribution of other provinces Well, that is a very large question, and the hon. gentleman can argue almost anything he likes from that statement, because it is hard to prove a statement of that kind.' I do not think it is so myself, and I say so frankly and fearlessly after a very long investigation into the question. I do think that the province of British Columbia is a very large contributor to the revenues of the Dominion, but that is aside from the issue altogether. Hon. gentlemen opposite have said that public works are not being carried on in the province of British Columbia by this government, but I would like to know what demands made upon this government for public works have been refused. What demands have this year been made on the^ government for necessary public works in that province which have been refused? To my knowledge, I know of none.
I can tell you.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I might point out to the hon, member (Mr. 'Cowan) that the very large and necessary public work of deepening the Narrows is provided for to just- as large an extent as it could be provided for. As much money is being provided for the coming year as can be well spent during the year. And so throughout the entire province, I know of no large public work which has been asked for that is not being done. The Fraser river, which is receiving a good deal of attention from my hon. friend from Westminster, is also being provided for, and the improvement of the channel up to Westminster is being carried out as rapidly as circumstances will permit.

The minister says that he knows of no public work that has

been requested that has not been provided Without going into many others, that 1 could mention, I would like to ask him with respect to two, which I myself heard him promise at a public meeting at Chilliwack during the last campaign, namely, a new post office for Chilliwack, another public building for Chilliwack, and dredging for Chilliwack, a dredge being then supposed to be actually on its way up the river. I am bound under the rules of the House to take the hon. minister's denial if he says that he did not promise these, although I heard him promise them myself. I ask him whether he has ever asked for these or whether they have been granted.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: This is extraordinary, Mr. Chairman. In the first place, I think I am as non-committal in making promises of public works in a constituency or as to the performance of anything in the future over which I have not absolute control, as any other member of the government, and I deny absolutely that 1 made any such promises at a public meeting at Chilliwack. But it is a fact that a site for a post office was being considered at that time, if it had not been secured, and if there was not in the estimates a sum of money for a post office at Chilliwack, it was certainly intended that there should be, and if I am not mistaken, it is in the estimates to-day.
It is there.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Votes for public buildings at Chilliwack, Vernon and two or three other places in British Columbia were cut out of the estimates last year in consequence of the general reduction oi the votes for public works. But I believe that these are in the estimates of this year.
I may have said that I was personally desirous of seeing a public building, and would use my best efforts to-have it built. If I made a casual promise of that kind, that promise is being fulfilled. As to the dredging in the Fraser river, that is a purely local question. I do remember something about the moving of a dredge from one point to another point to do a little local work. Whether that has been done or not I do not know. It certainly was intended to be done. But I know of no wharf, no dredging, no public building or other public work that should be carried out in the province of British Columbia that has not been carried out when proper representations have been made, and 1 challenge my hon. friends to say anything to the contrary. The province of British Columbia has not many towns or cities; but in almost every town of two or three thousand people and over we have now a nice public building, whereas when this government came into power there was only one public building if I am not mistaken.
certainly not more than two, in the entire province.

May I ask the minister a question? I presume that he knows that the tonnage of the port of Vancouver is second only to that of Montreal. Can he point to one dollar of Dominion money that has been spent in the improvement of that port?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The question is quite an unnecessary one. There is no better harbour in the_ Dominion than the harbour of Vancouver, and therefore it is unnecessary to spend much money to improve that harbour.
We have done dredging there. We have had the ' King Edward ' at work there.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The great improvement which the port of Vancouver requires is to widen and deepen the narrows, and I believe it is the intention of the Minister of Public Works- to buy a dredge for that work. In the last two or three years, one of the finest public buildings in Canada has been put up in Vancouver for a post office and custom house, and we have recently bought a tract of ground for an ex->
amining warehouse in connection with the custom house. We have provided all the accommodation in the way of public buildings that is necessary for the great city of Vancouver, and I am proud to say that it is a great city. It is all very well for my hon. friends to make statements in a general way, but they cannot substantiate them. I do not know what more we could get in the city of Vancouver. The deepening of the Fraser river from its mouth up to above Westminster is a very important work on which this government has already spent half a million dollars, and which it will take years to complete. In the city of Victoria we have been spending at least ten times as much money as did the former government, and in this year's estimates, there is twice the sum appropriated last year for the purpose of deepening some points in the harbour in order to accommodate the increase in shipping. It is all very well for my hon. friend to raise the miserable old issue, raised in the last general elections in British Columbia, of the alleged antagonism of this government to the best interests of British Columbia. That charge is a false one, and I challenge my hon. friend to make it good.

I accept that challenge, and I say further: perish my right hand if I ever in this House utter one statement I am not absolutely sure is correct. If I am right in saying that there is discrimination * against British Columbia, 'the government are absolutely unjust to that pro-vnee. The minister says T am wrong, but

I base my statement on figures, not prepared by myself, but by the Dominion's statistician, and they are absolutely correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I dispute that absolutely.

Very well, then grant an inquiry. Will the minister agree to that? I would like an answer. If the Dominion statistician will certify to the correctness of my figures, will the minister grant an inquiry?
Which minister?
Any minister-one or all. Will any minister say that if the Dominion statistician will certify to my figures, he will support my demand for an inquiry?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The proposition is too preposterous and ridiculous to entertain it for a moment. If British Columbia has any claim to any public works of the same class as is provided in any other part of Canada, that claim will receive consideration; but this pretense that one province pays more than another, is one of the ridiculous things we are apt to hear in this parliament. Why, my hon. friend from East Grey will remember when the province of Ontario was troubled with the conviction that it was the milch cow of the Dominion and had to pay for all the other provinces. We have heard Montreal plead the immense contribution it makes to the Dominion treasury because the imports for the west pass through it and the duties are there collected. But these duties are in reality paid by the people further west who consume the bulk of these imports. The same remark applies to Halifax and other ports of entry, so that no statement which could be prepared on the basis of the duties collected at the different ports could give a correct idea of the contribution to these duties by different sections of the country. The goods landed atone port may be consumed a thousand miles away, and it is the consumer a thousand miles distant who pays the tax, and not the importer at Halifax, St. John, Vancouver, Montreal or Quebec. No calculation that can be made on that subject can possibly be absolutely correct, but must be a matter of conjecture. It would be ridiculous to have an inquiry into a matter of that sort; but if British Columbia requires a public work of the same class as is provided by the Dominion in other provinces, and which i3 necessary and useful for the development of trade, then let that claim be brought forward, and if it be not considered then, and not until then, will British Columbia have a grievance.

I am very much pleased, indeed, that one of the ministers has had
the courage to speak out, but I regret the lack of that courage in the Minister of Inland Revenue. The Minister of Finance says that if there be discrimination-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say any thing about discrimination.

Against British Columbia

	1

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say that.
And the amount of that discrimination is certified to by the Dominion statistician-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said nothing of the kind.

Still he says he will grant us no inquiry. Yet this is the minister who in 1886 carried Nova Scotia for the repeal of the union, because that province was not getting fair treatment at the hands of the Dominion. When, however the other man's ox is gored', he gets up, brave as a lion, and says, no, I will give you nothing. Fortunately we can retaliate, to the extent of seven representatives in this House, on any minister who will defy us in that way. Let me say to the Minister of Finance that I know whereof I speak. I say there is a black injustice being done British Columbia, and that it reflects nothing to the credit of the Minister of Finance,.or hi3 government, to refuse an inquiry. We are prepared to take the results of that inquiry, let it be absolutely fair and impartial. If we can establish no right, if we cannot make good our claim, we will take the result and take it like men, but I cannot understand how any minister of any government can close the door of justice to any province or any portion of the people. We do not ask anything more than that we should have a fair and impartial hearing on this claim. The minister says that that is ridiculous, and what reason does he give. He says that the goods may be entered at Vancouver, but they may be consumed down at Halifax.
Hear hear.

And the minister's echo says ' Hear, hear.' But if the Minister of Customs were here, he could tell my hon. friend that the goods entered at the port of Vancouver-the through freight-do not pay duty at the port of entry, and if he would take the trouble of going to the office of the Dominion statistician he would learn that I am absolutely right and accurate in my statement that we can ascertain exactly how much that province is paying per head of its population into the Dominion treasury. I said exactly; I want to modify that to this extent, that

there are certain goods going north to the Yukon which leave a little shade of doubt as to the exact amount, but none of the goods going through east or anywhere else than north to the Yukon leave any shade of doubt. Thus his reason for saying, ' no ' does not anneal to me as cogent. If that was the strength of the reasons he advanced in 1886 for the repeal of the Union and the secession of Nova Scotia, I do not wonder that the result was changed in 1887.
I wish to assure the minister that I am not raising this point for any purpose other than this, that British Columbia should get a fair, impartial, just hearing of a claim that she thinks is just. It may be that we are wrong, it may be that we have no claim. We are not saying that we have a claim, that we have proved it conclusively; I can say that I know it is proven conclusively, but I am not asking you to accept my word; I am asking you to give British Columbia an impartial tribunal before which that claim may be heard. No man will refuse that-I cannot understand why the exigencies of party-
The hon. member does not oppose this item at ah?

No: but I must surely have an opportunity to reply to the Finance Minister's emphatic ' no ', and his unemphatic reason for saying ' no.' I would really like the Minister of inland Revenue to offer his testimony . as to whether he would be in favour of British Columbia having a fair and impartial hearing upon this claim or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I wish another word first. I think that if the hon. member felt that he had a good case in British Columbia he would hardly have travelled to the other end of the continent and introduced Nova Scotia. I have settled that question with my friends, with my Tory friends from Nova Scotia, over a long period of years, and there is nothing to be gained by reopening it. I have no reason to regret anything that happened. If I am to treat the hon. gentleman's remarks as serious, what is his proposal? That there shall be an inquiry as to whether or not British Columbia gets back all she pays. What reason is there that British Columbia shall have that inquiry? Why shall not the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) demand a similar inquiry _ for Ontario? Why shall not my hon. friends from Manitoba, from Prince Edward Island, from Quebec, why shall not the Minister of Public Works and the hon. member for Westmoreland demand a similar inquiry for their provinces?
And if their claims are just why should they not be heard?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then it means that we want to find out whether every province gets back 100 per cent on the dollar in actual direct payment-and that is provincialism run mad.
What harm would it do to find that out?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I say that this country is not being run on provincial lines; there must be give and take between the provinces. If every province is to be measured, if you are to show that a given province has paid $100 revenue and must get back $100. it is a ridiculous thing, and you never could make a nation on any such ground.

I never suggested that we should get 100 cents on the dollar back. There is not a ghost of a show of our getting that as long as there is in power a ministry that gives the money of this country to the big vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And as the hon. gentleman has no hope of seeing any other ministry I do not blame him for being anxious on the subject.
Still I think they might at least correctly report my statement and not misreport it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think I mis-reported my hon. friend, but I would be glad if he would tell me any reason why an inquiry should be granted to British Columbia and refused to Prince Edward Island, why
Possibly Prince Edward Island has not asked for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Prince Edward Island thinks it has a grievance. My hon. friend from Kings county tells us it has a grievance and I have heard Ontario members represent again and again that their province is the great taxpaying province of the Dominion.
Did not Nova Scotia set up the same claim?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Nova Scotia set up that claim at one time.
And successfully?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was a great many years ago, and the government of the day recognized Nova Scotia's claims many years ago by an additional amount.
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But does my hon. friend contend that the position of British Columbia is the same?
Much stronger.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If we have to go to ancient history, the great difference is this:

Nova Scotia did not enter the -union volund tariiy and she had a right to complain if she wanted to. British Columbia and the other provinces came into the union vol-untarilv; they made their bargain and would have no right to play the baby act if that bargain was enforced. All they have a right to say is that they are citizens of this Dominion and should be treated like other citizens. But it will not make for good government, it will not make for nationality, if we are going to take a tape-measure to find whether one province pays a dollar and gets back only ninety-nine cents.
The minister has asked why British Columbia should prefer a claim and the other provinces should not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I did not say that, I said why should they have an inquiry more than any other province; they can
make all the claims they like.

Since the question is put to me I wish to answer it. British Columbia has a right to an inquiry, because every trust transferred from the colony of British Columbia to the Dominion is being abused, and I venture to say it is being abused in such a way that if we could get into a court of equity we could get justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is a court of
equity.
But a court of equity that closes its doors; when we come rapping on the door, they say: No, no entrance here.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no, you are here.
The fountain of justice is closed. We are denied an impartial hearing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is in the position that he cannot get a judgment in his favour and so he says the fountain of justice is closed.

The minister says that because we came in voluntarily in 1870, therefore, we made a bargain. I do not know from what pettifogging lawyer he got the idea that a treaty is a contract. I did not know until I heard it from the Minister of Finance that a treaty such as the terms of union between British Columbia and the Dominion of Canada was a mere contract, and if we got the worst of the bargain we could squeal, but we must take our medicine. That is the position, the little position, the minister, takes. Men who have studied these things know that it is not a statesmanlike position to take upon this question. The intention of the union was that there should be without undue taxation sufficient revenues left to the
province to enable it to perform the duties assigned to it as a province under the terms of union and that the Dominion should only take such revenues away from the province-and that is the trust-as would enable the Dominion to perform the added duties imposed on the Dominion because of the province coming into confederation. So the Dominion is in the position of trustee of the powers of imposing indirect taxation.

If the hon. - gentleman would permit me to interrupt him, I would ask him whether it is really fair, on this item of $14,500 for improvements upon the Columbia river, to go into the question of the amendment of the British North America Act so as to give to British Columbia a larger subsidy than it now receives. What do you think, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not understand that the point of order has been raised.
Yes, it is a point of order.
In speaking to the point of order, I think this discussion is logical.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The point of order being raised, it is the right of the hon. member for Vancouver to explain what he desires to say.

I was induced to rise to my feet by the statement of the Minister of Public Works that he was unaware that there was discrimination against British Columbia, and he seemed to think that that negative statement, that ignorance which he alleged in himself, was s- ;ne reason for the argument he was advancing.

I think my hon. friend will realize that the question of an appropriation for a necessary public work in British Columbia is a very different question from that as to whether the British North America Act should be amended. They are two different questions. I am not aware that there is any discrimination against British Columbia.
No one knows better than the Minister of Public Works, because he is a capable lawyer, that no amendment is needed to the British North America Act.

Speaking on the point of order, I think any member of this House, in speaking of expenditures In his own province or elsewhere, if he thinks he is not getting a proportionate share of the finances that his province requires, can make a comparison between what is spent in his province and what is spent in any other province, on any item that is under consideration.

I would appeal to my hon. friends from British Columbia to allow these estimates to go ahead, because these are all necessary items.
Coquitlam river-removal of obstructions,
We wish to remove these obstructions so as to facilitate navigation.
This is one of the public works we have been asking for. Is there anything special being done on that river?

We had an appropriation for the present year, and up to the 31st of November we have spent $691. We are now asking for $1,000 more, which we intend to use for removing obstructions which exist to free the floating down of logs and shingle bolts. We hope to be able to effect a substantial improvement with this money. There have been some complaints' as to the results which have been obtained by past expenditures. We hope that this money will accomplish good work in removing those obstructions.
When were the complaints made?
I received a complaint not very long ago. I think I also have a letter from my hon. friend on the subject.

For the information of the Minister of Inland Revenue, who does not know that there is anything required in British Columbia at present, I would like to state that this complaint was sent from Coquitlam about the 16th of December. I will read a copy thereof:
To the Hon. the Minister of Public Works, Ottawa.
We, the undersigned, mill-owners of New Westminster, interested in logging, and residents of the municipality of Coquitlam being land owners along the banks of the Coquitlam river, do respectfully ask you to make an inquiry regarding the work which has been done to improve the channel of this river, for the last five years, by the money you have from time to time voted for that purpose.
Both banks have been slashed, and all overhanging trees cut down and limbed and thrown into the river, with the result that the river channel was covered over with a net work of scrub mattresses on which sand bars have formed, thus forcing the river out of its natural channel, and is doing immense damage to property on both banks.
This makes it very expensive and difficult to drive logs even during a freshet, as they either lodge on the sand bars in the centre channel or get jammed in the irregular side channels.
We respectfully lay this matter before you, as the river has got ouc of all control, and unless these reinforced sand bars are removed by dredging or other means great damage will result from every freshet.

After inspection we humbly trust you will see your way to supplement your granc for this year, as it is altogether inadequate to meet the improvements required.
If the minister has acted upon this he will have to supplement the vote, I suppose, in the supplementary estimates. If he has done that, it is no use my taking up the time, of the committee further. But if not, I think this is the proper time for , discussion. Does the minister propose to make a supplementary grant for the Coquitlam river?

It is quite impossible for me to inform my hon. friend even as to whether there will be any supplementary estimates. When the estimates are brought down, assented to by His Excellency the Governor General and submitted to the House, my hon. friend will know what they contain, but until that time, very much to his regret, I am quite sure, I am unable to give my hon. friend that information.

That may be a satisfactory answer from the minister's standpoint, but from the standpoint of an independent member of this House endeavouring to do his duty to his constituents, it is not a satisfactory answer. I do not think it is the answer that a member of this House, acting on behalf of his constituents, ought to receive. I do not think we are sent here to trifle in this manner with the public business. When a member comes down from a riding, presents a numerously signed petition from his constituents and which _has been in the hands of the minister for more than three months, asking for an appropriation for this work to avert threatening damage, the minister fails in his duty in standing up in this committee in this cavalier manner and making what is intended to be a smart observation that we shall learn what is in the supplementary estimates when they come down. I am quite as well aware of that as the minister is, and I do not thank him for the information at all. This only emphasizes the gross neglect of the interests of British Columbia by the Minister of Public Works, by the government iand by the Minister of Inland Revenue, who is supposed particularly to represent British Columbia and who told us a few minutes ago that there were no unanswered requests for improvements in British Columbia. To my own knowledge thousands of dollars of damage is being done to private property along the Coquitlam river every year by the ravages of the stream because of the insufficient attention given by this department to the matter of controlling the Coquitlam river. As the people say in their petition this money is wasted because of its insufficiency. A thousand dol-

lars a year will do nothing substantial towards the improvement of the Coquitlam river, and if we are going to save ' these people from damage the government will have to take more vigorous steps than any appropriation of a thousand dollars will enable them to take. I call this matters again to the attention of the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Inland Revenue, the representative of British Columbia who speaks without knowledge when he says that no requests frqpi that province remain unanswered.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know anything about the special merits of thisl work and I do not presume to speak of it, but I might inform the hon. gentleman that he is entirely mistaken when he assumes that the answer of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works could have been given in any other way. The answer of the Minister of Public Works is the answer which he is obligeu io give in and out of the House to innumerable requests. It is utterly impossible for the government to determine in advance what the supplementary estimates shall contain. Until these estimates are laid before parliament they are subject to revision and perhaps rejection. Not only did my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works intend no discourtesy to the hon. member, but he gave the proper answer when he said he was not able to tell him what might be in the supplementary estimates. That is the proper answer, and that is the a'nswer that we have to give to people every day.

There are ways and ways of giving an answer in parliament. It would have been a simple matter for the minister to say politely that he could not indicate what was going to be in the supplementary estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is not that what he did say?
No sir.
What did he say?
His answer was a very supercilious answer intended to make a laughing stock of the member who asked the question.
The hon. member is too sensitive altogether; he is supersensitive.

The hoti. member is not too sensitive, but I do not propose while I stand here on behalf of my constituents to accept an answer which is not a proper one. I guarded myself by stating in advance that if the minister could indicate that he was dealing with this matter in the supplementary estimates or otherwise I would not pursue the subject. Surely that was a proper request to make. I said if the minister was dealing with this
I would say no more. But the minister stands up and gives a smart and flippant answer.
I am exceedingly sorry that my hon. friend is so sensitive. I wonder if he wants to provoke a quarrel with myself as head of the Department of Public Works, I can assure him that if he does-
Is that a threat?

He is not taking a course which would commend itself to reasonable men. What the hon. gentleman asked me was to tell him whether a further amount for the Coquitlam river would appear in the supplementary estimates. I do not know that I have shown any discourtesy towards the hon. gentleman by telling him that I could not state even if there would be any supplemetary estimates and that I would be unable to tell him what these supplementary estimates would contain until they had actually received the assent of the Governor General and were actually submitted to the House. If the hon. gentleman says however that this amount of $1,000 which is in the estimates will be utterly wasted, will be of no use whatever, on the Coquitlam river, it raises the very serious consideration for myself as to whether we should spend any part of this appropriation .upon the Coquitlam river. My predecessor, in determining to make improvements^ on the poquitlam river, stretched a point in his desire to assist the people. Coquitlam is not a navigable river. It is a river which may be called a floatable river, down which logs are floated, and it must have been for my predecessor a serious question as to whether an amount should be placed in the estimates. In view of the fact that the hon. gentleman says that this money will do no good, that it has been wasted in the past, that it has been productive of no results and that it will be productive of no results in the future it raises the important question as to whether any portion of this appropriation shall be used for this purpose.

I wish to state that, to use a sporting expression, that cock does not fight. I am not at all terrorized by the threat of the hon. gentleman to withdraw this appropriation from the Coquitlam river. I presume that it was placed in the estimates in pursuance of what he considered to be his public duty. I do not presume that, it having been so placed there, the Minister of Finance, or the Postmaster General, or the minister from British Columbia will permit him to withdraw it for the unworthv reason stated, because it is not a matter for the Minister of Public Works alone. It is a matter for the government. I do not presume that they will permit him to say that he will withdraw it as a threat against any mem-

ber of this House who is pursuing his duty. I wish to correct again the minister in the statement that I said this would be entirely useless. I told him that this was altogether insufficient to procure the effective results which should be procured on the Coquitlam river. Even $50 or $100 could be used * to advantage there, and $900 can be used to advantage. But, the minister has not been using this appropriation in a way which would bring advantage from the ' expenditure; there are ways however in which it can be used.

I did not intend my remarks should be regarded as a threat, but I feel bound to take any hon. member of this House seriously, and when he alleges, as I understood my hon. friend to allege, that this amount would be practically useless unless we had a larger sum, I felt I was bound to take him seriously as a representative of that constituency, when tire constituency, through him, spoke as it did speak to-night, and said it would be utterly useless to expend this money.
I rise to a point of order. I object to the minister misquoting my remarks, particularly as I have explained just now what I said.
I was referring to what the hon. gentleman had said previously.
- TAYLOR. I rise to a point of order.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman's declaration of what he said must be accepted.

Of what he said previously. Then, all I can say is that I did not feel that it was out of place for me to take the hon. gentleman seriously, and any remarks which I made were the result of my so regarding the observations of the hon. gentleman.
Eraser river-(lower) wing darn, bank protection works, inclusive of repairs, $35,000.

This is to make further provision to maintain existing works from the city of Westminster to the Straits of Georgia, preventing the formation of detrimental side channels, protecting banks from erosion, also services in connection with the maintenance of navigation in this river.
Has the minister received a communication from the city of New Westminster lately in respect to this work, and what action, if any, has been taken upon the communication?

I did receive a communication from the city of New Westminster as to going on with the very large works of importance which had been laid out, and which consist not only of the Mr. J. D. TAYLOR.
-dredging, but also of the building of jetties for the purpose of giving direction to the channel and so improving the navigation.

Has the minister done anything in pursuance of the indication he gave to a public meeting at New Westminster last summer, that he might put two shifts a day on the dredge 1 Fruh-ling ' in order to obtain more effective work from it?	.
I am not sure that I addressed a public meeting at New Westminster, I do not think I did.
If the minister wishes to be very exact, it was a meeting of citizens and the board of trade.

Yes, it was not a large meeting; it was a meeting of the members of the board of trade. I did state that I intended to make provision for working the ' Fruhling ' two shifts per day, and the estimates we have before the House provide this very service. We hope to have two crews working on the ' Fruhling ' so as to do the work with the greatest rapidity possible.
When does the minister expect to have the channel upon which he is now working available for traffic ?
No one can- tell in a work of that kind when there are shifting sands. It is a very large work, but we hope, in the comparatively near future, to have the channel in good order.

I put a question on the order paper the other day, and I thought possibly that if the answer to it was given seriously by the minister he would remember it now. I am sorry he does not remember what time he told me then, because he placed the date so near in the future that I was more encouraged by it than by the reports I heard from New Westminster. The people of New Westminster are very anxious indeed about the progress of this work, and on the 7th of January of this year the board of trade at New Westminster addressed a petition to the Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier on this subject. I presume that petition found its way to the Minister of Public Works. It reads as follows: _
To the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier,
G.C.M.G., P.C., Ottawa.
Sir,-The New Westminster Board of Trade deems it necessary to again bring to the attention of your government the matter of the Fraser river ship channel.
The board desires to express its appreciation of the work done so far by the new ' Fruhling ' dredge, without which the channel at its entrance, would probably have become . impassable for ocean vessels of any size. As it is, however, it is only when the high tides

occur in daylight that vessels drawing 22 or 23 feet can pass in or out, the latter draught being the limit that may safely attempt the channel at all at the present time.
The usual volume of ocean traffic on the river has been maintained during the past year, but various large industrial propositions have been and are deterred from locating on the river by the fact that much time may be lost by vessels having to await daylight tides to enter and clear. As cases bearing on this point it may be mentioned that the board recently received a communication from the agents of the Blue Funnel line of steamships, plying direct between Liverpool and Vancouver, intimating that upon assurance of the adequacy of the channel for their vessels, they are desirous of sending them to this port ; also that a vessel chartered to deliver a cargo of iron pipe at this citv due to arrive in March next, will not be able to come here, as there will not be sufficient water for her on the Sand Heads.
To accommodate the trade now offering, it is imperative that a channel be provided without delay, sufficiently deep for the passage of the largest vessels plying on the Pacific ocean, at any stage of the tide, and buoyed and lighted so as to be navigable by day or night.
The board is of the opinion that to attain this result within a reasonable time, it will be necessary to either augment the dredging power now available for use on the river, or to proceed at once with the construction of a jetty from Garry Point to the outer edge of the Sand Heads, as suggested and recommended in reports heretofore submitted, on behalf of the citizens of New Westminster for the consideration of your government.
The board earnestly hopes that this matter will receive the immediate and favourable consideration of your government, and that provision will be made at this session of parliament for the vigorous prosecution of the work necessary to this end.
The minister will see from that, that there is more than ordinary interest taken in the carrying on of this work rapidly, because there is a great deal of shipping that would be headed for the Fraser river if there was any reasonable assurance of its getting in there. There are some very large industries there, and particularly to the new industries established at New Westminster it is a very serious matter that those interested should have to bring in their freight by any other route than by the Fraser river.
Fraser river-to refund to the municipality of Delta one-half their expense of constructing emergency works to protect the south bank of the river near Ladner's Landing, on condition chat the government of British Columbia will refund the other half, $1,850.
Why the division?

I think it was Mr. John Oliver who saw me on behalf of the municipality, and he said they had an assurance from the provincial government that they would pay half the cost of this work, provided my department would pay the other half, and therefore I put the vote in in that way.
Harbours, rivers and bridges-general repairs and improvements, $10,000.

In connection with this vote I have pleasure in further refreshing the memory of the Minister of Inland Revenue as to works applied for in the province of British Columbia and not granted. I see nothing in the estimates about a work to which I refer now, and so I must presume it has not received the attention of the government. I have here a letter which bears every evidence of authenticity, and which reads:
I wish to call your attention once more to the need of removing the obstructions to navigation in the Upper Lillooet river. All our farming implements and heavy goods that we cannot take in on horseback we have to bring by the Harrison and Lillooet lakes and the Upper Lillooet river, and it is almost impossible to get boats up the river. There are so many log jams in the river that men are in great danger of losing their lives in trying to get these goods up the river in boats. The government spent a few thousand dollars in removing log jams in the river in 1908 with very good results. We wrote to Mr. Templeman requesting him to try and get a grant for the above work. In his reply he said he would do all he could to comply with our request. We sincerely trust you will do all you can to get the government to remove log jams from the river, as it would be a great benefit to this settlement.
I would like to ask the minister whether he has given any attention to this case of the Upper Lillooet, which is before the government not only now, but was before it last year, on application from the same man who has written this letter?
I may say to my hon. friend that I have given consideration to the matter.
The minister has given consideration to it, but will Mr. Punch get any result?

I cannot tell my hon. friend that. But this item will be available for that work, and I recognize the Lillooet river as a navigable river where improvement of the navigation might very well be done. My department has done work there already, and out of this very vote I trust that we shall be able to make further improvements during the coming season.

There is another item which has been before the government for some time. I took the liberty of mentioning it to this House last year, and the minister promised me then that he would give it attention. That is the matter of improving the Fraser river be-

tween Chilliwack, the head of navigation, and Agassiz. I pointed out to the minister that on account of the river having been allowed to silt up between those two points, it is impossible to get navigation into Agassiz. This is a matter of recent date, because when this government took over the affairs of the Fraser river, navigation extended to Yale, which is far above Agassiz. I pointed out that the people of Agassiz were very much in the position of those of Ste. Croix, mentioned this afternoon, in that it was very advisable for them to make their shipments by water, but that it was impossible for vessels to get to the place. I suggested to the minister a very small appropriation for snagging between Chilliwack and Agassiz, and a provision for some sort of wharf at Agassiz, almost the cheapest kind that he could construct, so that these people might have relief from what they consider the excessive freight rates of the railway and send out their produce by steamer to New Westminster. I would like to ask the minister what has been done between last session and the present in the direction indicated.
I think my hon. friend must be wrong in his statement that I said I would give attention to this matter, if he takes that to mean that I would do it.
No, the hon. minister did not promise it.

Nothing has bfeen done between that time and the present that I am aware of; but perhaps we might be able to do it out of this vote. I will have the matter looked into, and see if we can use a part of the money for that purpose.

When did the government adopt the policy of doing no further work in the way of protecting the banks of streams? Has it been adopted within the last year or two, or has it been in force a considerable length of time?

I may say that since I have been Minister of Pubic Works I have been thinking the matter over, having regard to the largely increasing demands being made on the government. My colleagues and I have discussed the matter somewhat. We all recognize that if it were our duty to do work of this character, it would involve the.wDominion in very large expenditure. While we have not shut, down on this work entirely, we are limiting it largely to matters in connection with works that have been already entered upon. In the very items under discussion some work of this character in British Columbia is being provided for, but I am endeavouring to curtail our ex-Mr. J. D. TAYLOE.
penditure for this class of work as much as possible.

Perhaps the elections
had something to do with that. The minister had an appropriation for protecting the banks of streams of my constituency- in fact, protecting government property- and he withdrew it after the elections of 1908 were over. Was it because the constituency did not deliver the goods to the government on that occasion?

I would like to call the minister's attention to another matter which was before his department, a request for assistance which was not granted, and as to which the Minister of Inland Revenue has no knowledge. This comes from Mr. William Wilson, of Cottonwood island, near Chiliwack, who says he has been petitioning for two or three years in regard to the devastation of his farm by the current indue id by the formation of a bar in the Fraser river opposite his place, a bar which would be removed if the suggestion which I make with regard to navigation to Agassiz were carried out. Mr. Wilson reports that the matter went so far that Mr. Kickbush, the gentleman in charge of the government work there, brought up the assistant district engineer, Mr. Gauvreau, who spoke of dredging through the bar. Mr. Wilson also reports that a petition to the government was being circulated at that time-the 22nd of November last. I wonder if the minister proposes to do anything in the matter of this protection work at Chiliwack?

I have not thought of that. When matters come up for consideration-, we will have to see what are the most urgent demands that can be met out of this general v-ote of $10,000. I regret- that I cannot say anything more to bay hon. friend to-night as to the matter.

I have another matter that I must bring to the attention of the minister. It is from the same locality, and is in connection with a request, not only for dredging, which would enable the river steamers t-o come up to the proper wharf, but, if the dredging cannot, be gob, for road improvements which would enable the traffic to come down to the spot on the river where it has to meet the steamer. When I mentioned this the other night, the minister stated that he had no request from Chiliwack for that purpose, and the only meaning that we could take from that was that if he had such a request, he would pay alteration to it and give it his kind consideration. I have here a memo from the Chiliwack Board of Trade which indicates the extent thev are suffering for lack of just such an improvement as I have in mind. The letter covering it reads as follows:	.

I beg to inclose herewith copy of report concerning conditions re the Fraser river landing at Chilliwack, and statistics in support of claims of the residents of this valley for an improvement in the condition of the same.
The facilities afforded merchants and farmers, the latter class forming the majority of the population, for the shipping of goods at the Fraser river landing are entirely inadequate and cause a great deal of "inconvenience, expense, and frequent loss to those engaged in business and the farmers.
The object of the inclosed report is to place in your hands some reliable information regarding the amount of business conducted in the Chilliwack valley, and setting forth the very_ inadequate assistance supplied for the facilitating of the same.
Trusting that this data will be of value to you in setting forth the claims of this district for an improvement of the existing conditions, I beg to remain, yours truly,
Then, their memorandum, which will give the minister a fair idea of the importance of the trade generally in the Chilliwack valley, read3 as follows:

Merchandise received and shipped at Fraser River Landings,
The amount of general merchandise received and shipped at the port of Cliilli-wack, on the Fraser river, for the year ending in July, 1909, comprises the large total of 26,474 tons.
The steamer ' Beaver/ operated by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, carried 16,474 tons, as per the returns given by the general freight agent, and the steamer * Ramona' and other boats operated by the Western Steamboat Compan3r of New Westminster, carried as near as can be ascertained by tne records furnished, about 10,000 tons.
Wharfs.
There is a government wharf at this port, situated at such a point that it is only available for use by the steamers for a few months in the year, and from a statement made by the steamboat officials, fully three-quarters of the freight handled has to be shipped and landed at a point more than a mile below the government wharf, owing to the fact that the water is too low to allow the steamers to reach their proper landing place. For many years this fact has been a source of great worry and hardship to the merchants and shippers of this valley, and it must be pointed out that the period of low water comprises the rainy season in the fall and the winter and spring. The bulk of the shipping is done by the farmers in the fall and winter, their shipments comprising fruit and vegetables of all kinds, potatoes in large quantities, hay and live and dead stock; and at the same time the merchants are receiving their winter stocks of merchandise, &e. In the winter and spring, there is still considerable shipping of hay, potatoes and other farm produce held over, while the merchants and dealers are receiving their summer stocks of merchandise, machinery, flour and feed, &e.,
so that during the period in which the government wharf is in commission, from the months of May to September, there is comparatively little shipping to be done. The accommodation provided at the nearest point at which the boats can reach during the low-water period is only of a temporary nature and is situated on a gravel bar; the rush of high water each spring usually destroying it.
Shelter is provided by a shed built on a scow, and in many cases perishable freight has to be left out in the wet owing to lack of room. Goods having left the care of the transportation companies are frequently damaged by exposure, and the merchants have therefore no claim for damages, and after coming, perhaps, many thousand miles, are liable to the most damage within three miles of their destination.
Owing to the nature of the gravel bar at which, as stated above, the bulk of the freight is landed and shipped, it is impossible to maintain a road that will stand the heavy traffic during the seasons when the best of roads get out of repair through wet and frost, and the hardship inflicted in hauling heavy, costly and bulky freight over practically a beach and along shelving banks is nearly unbearable, to say nothing of the dangers incurred in conveying passengers to the boats.
Time and time again have the Dominion government been appealed to to have the channel dredged and maintained

I would like to call the attention of the Minister of Inland Revenue to that:
-so that the wharf and sheds standing idle the greater part of the year can be used and this hardship now suffered by shippers and consignees alike be relieved, but nothing has been done except promises given to have matters remedied, and after great pressure being brought to bear, some temporary repairs to the inadequate shelter provided at the lower gravel bar.
Statistics.
That the district of Chilliwack, comprising the city and the fertile country surrounding it is an important one, and entitled to be relieved at the hands of the government from the condition of affairs with regard to better shipping and landing facilities on the Fraser river, is shown by some figures dealing with the post office, express shipments, &c., output of factories and population.
Population.
The population of the district, including the city of Chilliwack, which is incorporated, according to the last estimate made some time ago, is 5,500, but the next census will probably show larger figures, as new families are coming into the district every week.
Then follows a page of statistics which I shall not read. I would say, however, that I think the matter is sufficiently important to engage the attention of the committee even at this late hour of the night. An inspection of these statistics shows that the cost to the people of Chilliwack, because of the lack of facilities for making connections with steamboat traffic, is estimated on the rate per ton which they pay in addition

to the normal rate, and that amounts to $10,000 a year. That is the amount of tax levied on those people every year because of the neglect of this government to provide a work which probably all told would not cost what the people pay in one year. That is a matter which ought to have been within the knowledge of the Minister of Inland Revenue as representing British Columbia. It seems to me that it must have been within his knowledge. I have heard him address public meetings at Chilliwack. I know that he spent a whole day there, and I think he did make himself familiar with the surroundings. I am surprised, therefore, that he should tell the House that he knows of no application for assistance to this riding which has not been granted by this government. Why, the people are paying $10,000 a year as a special tax to make connections which the government should provide without this tax. This ought to be considered a matter of urgency, and the minister should make it a very special case, considering the number of years the people have be 3n suffering.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
When I challenged the representatives from the province of British Columbia to show that any application which had been made for public works in that province had been refused, I was referring, of course, to works of large magnitude and not to works such as the one to which my hon. friend refers. No one knows better than my hon. friend the - difficulties of the Fraser river, and I quite appreciate the difficulties under which the farmers of Chilliwack county suffer. It is true that certain wharf facilities are not available, but that is in consequence of the continual shifting of the river, the formation of sand bars, the washing away of banks and islands, the formation of new ones, and the continual changing of the channel. Right opposite the Chiliwack landing I will show broad areas of gravel bank, were some ten years ago a farm of 160 acres had existed that had been washed away. The Fraser river will always be a difficult problem for any government with respect to navigation and to construction of retaining works. I have discussed the matter frequently with Mr. Keefer, the resident engineer, and work has been done, but not probably of a nature sufficient to enable steamers to come to the present wharf. Mr. Keefer is most anxious to use the money voted for the Fraser river, so as to give the farmers all along the valley as far as Chilliwack all the facilities possible; and I am quite sure it is the intention of the department to carry out just that class of work to which my hon. friend refers. I repeat that when I made the statement that the representatives of British Columbia could not make good their Mr. J. D. TAYLOR.
challenge, I desired that they should point to some considerable public work which has been refused. There are here and there throughout the province, I know myself, places where wharfs ought to be built that are not in the estimates yet; we will have them there before very long. There are places on the Fraser river that should be dredged, and probably some places where wharfs should be built, but they are not very numerous and no doubt in a very short time all these wants will be attended to.

I must congratulate the Minister of Inland Revenue on the condition of affluence which he enjoys which makes him think that a public work -the absence of which costs the people of Chilliwack $10,000 a year-is not worth his lordly consideration.	.
I want to bring another need before his attention. I refer to the matter of aids to navigation on the Serpentine river, which serves the municipality of Delta, near the mouth of that river. This was undertaken many years ago, the minister of that_ day recognizing the importance of providing water transportation by the Serpentine river. In the course of years the work then done has become decayed. On September 24 last, this letter was addressed to the secretary of the board of trade of New Westminster who had interested himself on behalf of the petitioners:
Ottawa, September 24, 1909.
Sir,-I beg to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 11th inst., in reference to aids to navigation in the Serpentine river, and would advise you that Captain Gaudin referred your previous correspondence to this department promptly, with a recommendation that the piles formerly marking the channel of the Serpentine river should be replaced. The lowest offer Captain Gaudin could get for doing the work was $1,062, and besides which, the department would have to provide several buoys, and as the life of the piles from previous experience, appears to have been only two or three years, we question whether the traffic in the district would warrant so large an expenditure, and propose deferring action until a technical officer of the department can visit the locality and determine conditions on the spot. We have only a limited vote available for aids to navigation, and must spend the money where it will be an advantage to the greatest tonnage of shipping.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Signed) C. STANTON, Assistant Deputy Minister
of Marine and Fisheries. Chas. H. Stuart-Wade, Esq., F.R.G.S., Sec.-Treas. Board of Trade,
New Westminster, British Columbia.
Since this letter was written there has been ample time for the inquiry by a tech-

nical officer indicated. I would ask what the result of that inquiry has been.

My hon. friend is asking about matters with which the Minister of Public Works has nothing to do. This belongs to the Department of Marine and Fisheries and if my hon. friend would defer this matter until we get into the Marine and Fisheries items I have no doubt the acting minister would be very glad to give the information desired.
Haven't we been providing aids to navigation?
That is in the Marine Department.
You have been providing works like this?
No.
Some time ago I asked that the House should adjourn. I now ask the deputy Speaker to count the House out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, I would rather move the adjournment of the House.
Some resolutions reported.

I wish to ask the Finance Minister whether he could give any information as to negotiations with Washington respecting tariffs. I am informed there are press despatches from Washington indicating that something im-[DOT]portant is going on there and there is some public anxiety ta know whether the minister has any communication that can be made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The matter is not in a position that would permit me to make any intimation to the House at present.
What business will be taken up on Monday?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will proceed on Monday with the naval debate.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 12.20 a.m., Saturday.
Monday, February 28, 1910.
